title: Beyond Degrees: Understanding the Essential Role of IT Certifications in Modern Tech Careers
affiliations: Sinclair Community College, Trinity College (Toronto) and

detail.title: Beyond Degrees: Understanding the Essential Role of IT Certifications in Modern Tech Careers
detail.abstract: There is a growing necessity of professional IT certifications for technology practitioners across North America, highlighting their role as standardized indicators of competence in an industry defined by rapid innovation and evolving employer expectations. IT certifications function as formal validations of technical skills, complementing academic credentials by demonstrating proficiency with current tools, platforms, and security practices. Their increasing importance stems from employer demand for verifiable, job-ready capabilities, particularly in high-growth fields such as cloud computing, cybersecurity, and network administration, where certifications often serve as screening criteria or preferred qualifications. The opening section of this article explores the growing need for IT certifications and outlines the wide range of credentials available to both junior and senior technology professionals. Certifications also play a pivotal role in improving employment outcomes, as they enhance credibility, strengthen resumes, and help candidates especially newcomers and early-career professionals stand out in competitive job markets. However, the financial burden associated with certification exams, training materials, and renewals can pose challenges for students or professionals with limited financial resources. To address this, the later section of this article outlines practical strategies such as leveraging institutional discounts, employer-sponsored programs, government-funded upskilling initiatives, and free or low-cost learning platforms that enable individuals to pursue essential certifications without compromising financial stability.

title: When Cybersecurity Incidents Fail to Teach: Executive Attention and the Limits of Experiential Learning at the Board Level
affiliations: , University of Gdansk, University of Gdansk and Goethe University Frankfurt - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration

detail.title: When Cybersecurity Incidents Fail to Teach: Executive Attention and the Limits of Experiential Learning at the Board Level
detail.abstract: Research on organizational learning and information systems (IS) governance commonly assumes that adverse digital events improve senior decision-makers' understanding of risk. This study tests a necessary prediction of experience-based learning at the apex of the firm: if organizations learn from cybersecurity incidents, exposure must leave a detectable cognitive trace at the board level. Using cybersecurity incidents as a theoretically extreme case of rare, technically opaque, and expert-mediated IS failures, we examine whether recent incident experience is associated with board-level understanding of cyber-risk. Drawing on survey data from 144 senior cyber-risk professionals with sustained board exposure, we assess direct, indirect, and structurally amplified channels through which experiential learning could plausibly operate. Across all channels, we find no evidence that incident exposure is associated with higher boardlevel cyber-risk literacy. Instead, board cyber-risk literacy is strongly associated with sustained executive attention, reflected in CEO prioritization and recurring board airtime. Formal governance structures, including CISO proximity, do not add explanatory power once patterns of executive attention are considered. These findings constrain a core assumption of experience-based learning theories by showing that exposure to adverse events does not reliably generate detectable learning signals at the organizational apex. Under conditions of rarity, technical opacity, and expert mediation, experiential signals appear insufficient to produce an observable cognitive trace at the board level. In such contexts, sustained executive attention appears to function not as a mediator of experiential learning, but as an alternative pathway through which board-level learning occurs when experiential signals fail to become informationally viable.

title: Contract-Governed Adversarial Evaluator Hardening: Stage-Gated Recursive Improvement with Typed Promotion Contracts

detail.title: Contract-Governed Adversarial Evaluator Hardening: Stage-Gated Recursive Improvement with Typed Promotion Contracts
detail.abstract: When an adversarial evaluator is itself the object of recursive improvement, unconstrained optimization can soften the enforcement surface the evaluator is supposed to maintain. This paper describes a stage-gated architecture in which a deterministic meta-runner-no learned parameters, no language-model judgment-governs evaluator-hardening by executing precommitted Python promotion contracts that return PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED verdicts. Over a four-month development period, six evaluator-hardening stages were promoted through this mechanism. The contracts blocked one sloppy promotion before a fix was applied, scoped each stage to a named evaluation surface so that no stage could claim credit for improvements made elsewhere, and forced integration debts into separately governed programs rather than letting them inflate passing stage claims. The work builds on prior documentation of specification gaming in LLMgenerated code [Alami, 2025a] and evaluator hardening through mined failure constraints [Alami, 2025b]. All claims are scoped to one system operated by one principal; generalization requires independent replication.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the vulnerability and resilience of interconnected energy, communication, and livelihood systems under simulated Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) disruptions. While EMP research has traditionally focused on technical and military domains, limited attention has been given to its systemic and socioeconomic impacts at the community level. Using a mixed-methods design, this study examines how disruptions in energy and communication systems cascade into livelihood instability in selected communities in Biliran Province, Philippines. Data were gathered through surveys, system-mapping exercises, and scenario-based simulations. Results indicate that energy systems serve as the critical backbone, with communication and livelihood systems highly dependent on its functionality. Disruption's trigger cascading failures, leading to reduced income, information breakdown, and weakened adaptive capacity. The study proposes a socio-technical systems model for understanding technological risks and highlights the need for integrated resilience planning. Findings contribute to disaster risk reduction, sustainable development, and systems theory by emphasizing the interconnected nature of modern community vulnerabilities.

title: Bridging Assessor Subjectivity in CMMC Level 2
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bridging Assessor Subjectivity in CMMC Level 2
detail.abstract:
“Met can mean a control was demonstrated, tested, and confirmed. Met can also mean an IT administrator said it was configured and nobody checked. The current CMMC methodology records both outcomes the same way. The Promise State Framework proposed here records the difference.”

CMMC Level 2 assessments conducted under NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-171 Rev. 2 Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Non-Federal Systems and Organization, and the Defense Industrial Base Cybersecurity Assessment Center (DIBCAC) High Assessment methodology produce binary findings: a requirement is either Met or Not Met. This binary structure obscures critical operational reality assessors routinely make confidence judgments about evidence quality that are never captured in the formal record. Two assessors examining identical evidence for the same requirement may reach the same binary conclusion through fundamentally different levels of verification confidence, with no mechanism to distinguish between them.
This paper proposes applying Promise Theory, developed by Mark Burgess, as a structured framework for capturing assessor confidence at the practice level. The central mechanism is a three-state Promise State classification Verified, Assumed, or Unknown/Gap applied alongside the official NIST SP 800-171A Assessing Security Requirements for Controlled Unclassified Information determination. An illustrative example drawn from requirements 3.1.12 through 3.1.14 demonstrates how Promise State changes what an assessment record communicates.

title: The Rise of Stablecoins: A Comprehensive Analysis of Their Mechanisms, Impact, and Future in the Global Financial Landscape
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Rise of Stablecoins: A Comprehensive Analysis of Their Mechanisms, Impact, and Future in the Global Financial Landscape
detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive examination of stablecoins, a class of cryptocurrency designed to mitigate the price volatility inherent in major digital assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum. By pegging their value to stable assets such as fiat currencies, commodities, or through algorithmic manipulation, stablecoins aim to serve as a reliable medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value within the digital economy. Through systematic literature review methodology, this research traces the evolution of stablecoins, dissects their underlying mechanisms, and categorizes them into four primary types: fiat collateralized, commodity-collateralized, crypto-collateralized, and algorithmic. The paper analyzes their expanding use cases, from powering decentralized finance (DeFi) and revolutionizing cross-border payments to enhancing corporate treasury functions, while scrutinizing the significant risks they present, including de-pegging events, regulatory uncertainty, and systemic financial risks. The catastrophic collapse of the Terra/LUNA ecosystem serves as a critical case study, offering profound lessons on the vulnerabilities of algorithmic models. The research navigates the complex global regulatory landscape, comparing approaches from major jurisdictions including the United States GENIUS Act, European Union MiCA regulation, and UK FCA frameworks. By synthesizing market data, growth projections, and doctrinal analysis, this paper concludes with a forward-looking perspective on stablecoins' enduring role in the ongoing digitalization of finance and provides normative recommendations for balanced regulatory approaches that foster innovation while ensuring financial stability.

title: Memory-Governed Decision Systems: A Unifying Paradigm for Neuromorphic-Inspired Governance Across Heterogeneous Execution Surfaces
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Memory-Governed Decision Systems: A Unifying Paradigm for Neuromorphic-Inspired Governance Across Heterogeneous Execution Surfaces
detail.abstract: Contemporary AI systems are overwhelmingly compute-centric: architectures are evaluated by parameter counts, FLOP budgets, and inference throughput. We argue that the dominant failure modes of deployed AI-context loss across interactions, decision drift under distribution shift, cross-channel inconsistency, non-auditability, and fragmented governance-are fundamentally memory failures, not compute failures. Drawing on (i) the neuroscience of memory systems, (ii) neuromorphic computing principles where memory and compute are co-located and inseparable, and (iii) the operational demands of governing AI across heterogeneous execution surfaces, we propose Memory-Governed Decision Systems (MGDS): a system-level paradigm in which memory is versioned, policy-bound, auditable, and constitutive of downstream action authorization. We formalize MGDS as a four-tuple (M, P, D, A) with well-defined transition semantics, introduce a four-level taxonomy of memory substrates, lifecycle stages, governance layers, and execution surfaces, and present an implementable reference architecture comprising memory, governance, execution, and feedback planes. We draw a substantive analogy to neuromorphic event-driven computation, proposing neuromorphic-inspired governance mechanisms including event-triggered policy checks and plasticity-like memory update rules with audit constraints. We distinguish MGDS from adjacent categories-RAG, vector databases, feature stores, MLOps, policy engines, and agent frameworks-via failure-mode analysis and show that none subsumes the paradigm. We propose a benchmark suite with six task families, formal metrics, and baselines, provide a cost model for governed actions, present a threat model with mitigations, and develop a conceptual case study in omnichannel advertising governance for SMB merchants. Our central claim is falsifiable: if the failures enumerated can be resolved without first-class memory governance, the paradigm is unnecessary.

title: An Immodest Field Guide To The Pseudo-Species Of The Hype-Citation Economy

detail.title: An Immodest Field Guide To The Pseudo-Species Of The Hype-Citation Economy

keywords.keywords: academic publishing; epistemic inflation; falsifiability; Hype-Citation Economy; LLM-generated text; philosophy of science; pseudo-science; replication crisis; satirical taxonomy; theory-shaped text

detail.abstract:
This Guide is a work of scholarly satire in the tradition of Jonathan Swift’s A Modest Proposal (1729), applied to the contemporary knowledge economy. It argues that three structural developments — perverse incentive architecture, the prestige gradient, and the near-zero marginal cost of Large Language Model text production — have created an ecosystem in which theory-shaped text flourishes independently of empirical constraint. The result is the Hype-Citation Economy: a post-LLM scholarly landscape populated by pseudo-species that wear the costume of science while failing its criteria.

The Guide proceeds in four movements: a diagnosis of structural conditions; a benchmark standard drawn from Einstein and Mendeleev; a six-level hierarchy of epistemic artifacts (the Great Chain of Hollowness); and a formal taxonomy of eight pseudo-species, each described in the manner of the naturalist. A six-test diagnostic instrument — the Assay of Fool’s Gold — is provided for field identification, grounded in the philosophy-of-science traditions of Popper, operationalism, and predictive theory testing. The Guide is offered to working scientists and scholars, to historians and philosophers of science, and to anyone who has observed the phenomena described here but lacked the vocabulary to name them.

The Guide acknowledges its own limits: the infestation it describes is concentrated in specific ecological zones — interdisciplinary theory, speculative cognitive science, AI consciousness discourse — and does not represent a claim that all contemporary scholarship is epistemically compromised. It makes no claim to completeness. Taxonomy is a collaborative enterprise. This is a first edition.

title: Four Questions for Six LLMs  A Sequential Assessment of Engineered Intelligence
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Four Questions for Six LLMs  A Sequential Assessment of Engineered Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Six leading large language model systems—Claude Opus 4.6, Copilot, GPT, Gemini, xAI SuperGrok, and Perplexity AI—were subjected to a structured, sequential exercise requiring each to generate disciplinary questions for a hypothetical MIT symposium, rank those questions by importance, assess the actual design authority of the highest-ranked disciplines in production LLM pipelines, and perform a self-assessment of exhibited intelligence using the WAIS-IV framework. A second phase required each system to evaluate all six across seven comparative dimensions and to analyze the engineering difficulties of six “self-X” capabilities. Five principal findings emerged: (1) all systems converged on the structural irony that the disciplines most important to AI’s trajectory have no role in its production design; (2) every system diagnosed the epistemological deficit it embodies without resolving it; (3) self-assessments revealed a suggestive inverse correlation between self-assigned intelligence and demonstrated epistemic honesty; (4) beneath surface-level stylistic differences, all systems reproduced a shared consensus hierarchy; and (5) no system produced a genuinely original idea as measured against the criterion of transformational creativity. A real-time confabulation event during the exercise confirmed the architectural thesis: the token-prediction mechanism that makes these systems fluent is the same mechanism that makes them confabulate, and the systems have no internal means to distinguish the two modes. The findings support the necessity of the “maestro model” of transparent human-AI collaboration, grounded in the structural impossibility of generating epistemic warrant from within the autoregressive token-prediction architecture.

title: The Machine and the Maestro: Volume Pressure, AI-Mediated Admissions, and the Meritocratic Bifurcation in American Higher Education, 1990-2025
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Machine and the Maestro: Volume Pressure, AI-Mediated Admissions, and the Meritocratic Bifurcation in American Higher Education, 1990-2025

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
This paper advances a tripartite thesis about the transformation of American higher education between 1990 and 2025. The first movement is diagnostic: the admissions pipeline has shifted from meaningfully human-managed to substantially automated machine-managed, driven by application volume growth that outpaced human processing capacity and was met by an accelerating adoption of AI/LLM and related computational systems across every phase of the cycle. The volume-to-staffing arithmetic demonstrates the physical impossibility of meaningful holistic human review at current levels, supporting the inference that algorithmic systems now perform the determinative triage that human reviewers subsequently ratify. A crossover point (circa 2020–2022) marks the moment at which technology shifted from assistive to dominant. The second movement is structural: AI has become the substrate of the entire higher education business model, with demand-side AI (students using LLMs to produce applications) matched against supply-side AI (institutions using algorithmic systems to triage, score, and admit). The SAT/ACT—now being reinstated at elite institutions while remaining optional or absent at more than 2,000 others—emerges as the last externally verified demonstration of unassisted human cognitive capacity in the pipeline, creating a two-tier epistemic structure: a meritocratic bifurcation. The third movement is prescriptive: once the student cohort is onboarded, the Maestro Model—in which innate human intellectual capacity determines the quality of AI-assisted output, just as the quality of slide-rule work once depended on the operator’s mathematical competence—becomes the operating principle and the pedagogical framework of the post-AI university. The paper proposes that institutions must codify pre-tool ideation requirements, quality-of-use rubrics, faculty competence standards, and institutional assessment frameworks if the degree is to certify demonstrated intellectual capacity rather than mere participation in a machine-mediated process.

The paper employs a multi-system diagnostic methodology under the Maestro Model framework, directing seven generative AI systems as research instruments. The evidentiary architecture draws on application volume data (1990–2025), admissions staffing ratios, vendor technology documentation, institutional AI policies, the emerging regulatory landscape, business-model economics, and the current literature on AI-mediated assessment and credentialing. The paper’s claims are of two kinds—documented and inferential—and the distinction is maintained throughout.

title: Beyond Data-Driven Mobility: A Conceptual Framework for Autonomous Electric On-Demand Public Transit in European Urban Areas

detail.title: Beyond Data-Driven Mobility: A Conceptual Framework for Autonomous Electric On-Demand Public Transit in European Urban Areas
detail.abstract: European public transit is in structural crisis: 51% of European citizens never use public transport, rising to 68% in Italy [Eurostat, 2025]. Rome loses 76 hours/year to congestion (17th worldwide) and Milan 67 hours/year (24th) [INRIX, 2026]; social costs of road traffic reach approximately €34 billion/year [SIMA, 2024]; fuel and oil price volatility [IEA, 2024]. The dominant institutional response increasingly focuses on improving mobility data collection and analytics systems. This paper critically examines the epistemological limitations of such an approach and proposes a conceptual Autonomous Electric Demand-Responsive Transport (AEDRT) model as an alternative paradigm: a formal PDPTW model, microservices architecture, and conceptual simulation [SIM]. All simulation values are labeled [SIM] and are design hypotheses, not empirical data.

detail.title: Robots at the Gates? Robotic Process Automation, Skills and Institutions in Knowledge-Intensive Business Services

publicationDetails.detailsText: Digit Working Papers No. 04, University of Sussex, Sussex. https://dx.doi.org/10.20919/VUNU3389

detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of the fourth industrial revolution, this paper examines the emergence of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) as one of the new technologies that are shaping the future of work and reconfiguring sectoral business and innovation systems and models. It discusses how the institutional context can potentially mediate the digital transformation of services, how RPA affects workers’ employment and skills, and how it alters inter-organisational relationships and capabilities. Bringing together different strands of academic literature on employment studies, innovation, and technology studies, it deploys a comparative institutional perspective to explore the potential effects of RPA and illustrates their plausibility through mini case studies from knowledge-intensive business services.

title: Internet of Things - Supply Chain Industry Applications and Challenges

detail.title: Internet of Things - Supply Chain Industry Applications and Challenges
detail.abstract: Significant advancement in technology since the inception of internet has changed the way industries adopted advancement in technology to improve efficiency. One such important concept is Internet of Things, IOT also called the fourth wave of industrial revolution, Industry 4.0. Industries have vastly taken advantage of machine-to-machine interactions for automation like smart manufacturing, smart power grids, smart digital supply chains, connected logistics, connected assets, and preventive and predictive maintenance. IoT is increasingly being adopted across industries by leveraging the technological advancements in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning research positioning itself as a single source of truth in modern era of supply chain operations. The significant presence and importance of IoT makes it an essential research topic. This paper presents the development, significance, benefits, and challenges of IoT focusing on supply chain in various industries. This study emphasizes the influence of IoT on industrial operational factors that shape supply chain decision-making.

title: bat {AI}lle: On Acephalic Intelligence and the General Economy of Computation
affiliations: Episteme

detail.title: bat {AI}lle: On Acephalic Intelligence and the General Economy of Computation
detail.abstract: This essay sketches a Bataillean theory of contemporary artificial intelligence. It reads large-scale models and their infrastructures through Bataille’s general economy, treating AI as an engine of surplus expenditure that transforms energy, data, and desire into a secular form of the sacred. Drawing on the concepts of the accursed share, acephaly, eroticism, and inner experience, the essay argues that modern AI systems operate as acephalic intelligences: non-subjective formations that are technically distributed, institutionally concentrated, epistemically opaque, and behavior-governing. From this perspective, training and deployment appear as sacrificial procedures, while hallucinations and other excessive outputs emerge as forms of sovereign waste within a regime devoted to optimization. AI thus appears as a central ritual of capitalist expenditure, an altar on which energy, data, and subjectivity are offered in exchange for prediction, in a transaction that approaches prophecy. The essay therefore positions contemporary AI at the junction of computational rationality, capitalist expenditure, and the secular sacred, and asks what a politics of expenditure might become in an acephalic age.

title: The Idol Factory Multiple Points of Epistemic Failure Across Human-LLM Interaction Systems
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Idol Factory Multiple Points of Epistemic Failure Across Human-LLM Interaction Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
Large Language Models do not produce knowledge, reasoning, or logically grounded conclusions. They produce syntactically well-formed strings that exploit human pattern-recognition to simulate the appearance of reasoning. Once one applies the classical principle of garbage in, garbage out, the mechanism becomes clear: the model’s outputs are bounded by the quality and integrity of the patterns it has ingested. Because these systems are compression engines—lossy compression engines, in Shannon’s (1948) sense—what is discarded in the process is precisely provenance: the relationship between a token sequence and whatever worldly conditions made the original utterance true or false. The higher a system’s benchmark performance, the more dangerous it becomes—not because it reasons better, but because its inability to ground its own outputs becomes progressively undetectable. The result is a civilizational condition in which consequential decisions across medicine, law, military operations, and public policy are made on the basis of actionable guesswork—while the institutions making those decisions believe they are acting on knowledge.

This essay maps sixteen discrete points of epistemic failure across the full temporal lifecycle of human–LLM interaction, from training corpus construction through institutional uptake to retraining contamination and infrastructure dependency. It demonstrates, through an empirical exercise administered to seven systems, that the failures are uniform, structural, and architecturally inherent. It grounds the diagnosis in a genealogy running from the Torah’s prohibition against epistemic substitution through Bacon’s taxonomy of the Idols to the present industrial-scale manufacture of counterfeit epistemic signals. It argues that the condition has already crossed the threshold of reversibility: the systems are load-bearing infrastructure, not experimental instruments, and the question of whether to deploy is moot. The only remaining question is how to manage a civilizational condition that is already constitutive. Appendix D documents a second evidentiary exercise in which the expanded (v11) essay was submitted to five systems for review, scoring, and counter-argument; the systems produced more elaborate evasions but the same structural incapacity, confirming the thesis through the very responses intended to refute it.

title: Diagnostic Stress Testing of Seven Generative AI Systems -A Three-Round Meta-Layer Assessment Using Rubric Construction as a Novel Diagnostic Method
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Diagnostic Stress Testing of Seven Generative AI Systems -A Three-Round Meta-Layer Assessment Using Rubric Construction as a Novel Diagnostic Method

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Every major AI benchmarking protocol in the current literature—HELM, MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, BIG-Bench—works in the same direction: human researchers construct an evaluative instrument, and the systems are scored on their responses to it. This paper reverses that relationship. It makes rubric construction the test itself. Seven generative AI systems—Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT, Perplexity AI Pro, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.6, xAI SuperGrok, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Search—received identical instructions requiring each to build a scoring rubric, define its categories, rank all seven systems, and produce formatted output. In a second round, each system received all seven first-round outputs and was asked to synthesize them into a higher-order macro rubric. In a third round, the researcher conducted a meta-analysis of the second-round outputs. The methodological contribution is the demonstration that evaluation-construction tasks produce a categorically different kind of diagnostic evidence than evaluation-response tasks. Where conventional benchmarks measure what a system knows or which outputs humans prefer, rubric construction reveals evaluative disposition: whether a system exercises independent judgment or defers, whether it flags ambiguity or resolves it silently, and whether its self-assessment is calibrated or promotional. These behavioral signatures reproduced with striking consistency across rounds, suggesting they are structural features of current architectures rather than incidental artifacts. The paper proposes that evaluation-construction tasks merit inclusion in the standard benchmarking toolkit alongside evaluation-response tasks, because the two test different capacities and produce non-redundant diagnostic information.

title: Market Flexibility and Market Freeze in an Era of International Conflict: A Strategic Framework for Firms and Individuals

detail.title: Market Flexibility and Market Freeze in an Era of International Conflict: A Strategic Framework for Firms and Individuals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants or sensitive data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Markets do not stop during periods of disruption. What stops is the capacity of firms and individuals to move within them. This paper introduces the concept of Market Freeze a state of strategic paralysis in which organizations and individuals, confronted with geopolitical turbulence, trade disruption, and policy uncertainty, become unable to reposition, diversify, or mobilize resources, despite often having the means to do so. Market Freeze is not a consequence of resource depletion; it is a consequence of strategic arrest-the behavioral and structural tendency to defer adaptation rather than execute it. 
Drawing on authoritative evidence from the International Monetary Fund, World Trade Organization, OECD, UNCTAD, and the World Bank, published between 2024 and 2026, and building explicitly on the author's prior published research on war-driven marketing disruption (Radwan, 2025a) and market resilience under geopolitical stress (Radwan, 2025b), this paper develops the Radwan Market Flexibility Framework (RMFF)-a practitioner-oriented diagnostic and strategic guide for resolving Market Freeze conditions. The RMFF is organized around six flexibility dimensions: market diversification, offering adaptability, channel readiness, liquidity management, investment staging, and decision velocity. Each dimension is supported by diagnostic indicators, evidence-based corrective actions, and implementation guidance calibrated to both corporate entities and individual economic actors. 
The paper concludes with the Market Flexibility Score (MFS), a 35-point self-assessment instrument that classifies entities into four resilience tiers: Frozen, Vulnerable, Adaptive, and Resilient. The contribution of this paper lies not in cataloguing the effects of conflict on markets-a well-documented phenomenon but in providing a structured, actionable framework for maintaining commercial and economic mobility when the operating environment becomes hostile.

title: Trade Openness and Sustainability in Sri Lanka: Evidence from a Triple Bottom Line ARDL Evaluation of SDG-Aligned Development Pathways
affiliations: University of Sri Jayewardenepura, University of Sri Jayewardenepura and University of Sri Jayewardenepura

detail.title: Trade Openness and Sustainability in Sri Lanka: Evidence from a Triple Bottom Line ARDL Evaluation of SDG-Aligned Development Pathways
detail.abstract: Rapid globalisation creates growth opportunities, however, its environmental and distributional effects remain particularly uncertain for small developing economies with structural and institutional constraints. While trade is central to development strategies, many existing research examines economic, environmental and social outcomes separately, limiting its policy relevance. This study analyses the impacts of trade on Sri Lanka's economic growth, environmental quality and social equity from 1980 to 2023 using an Autoregressive Distributed Lag framework, providing the first country-level assessment integrating all three dimensions. The results show that trade liberalisation supports economic growth in the short run but does not generate sustained long-run effects due to structural constraints. Nevertheless, trade openness is not a significant driver of carbon emissions and environmental outcomes are shaped mainly by domestic energy Original Research Article composition and industrial activity. Socially, trade openness is associated with higher income inequality, indicating an uneven distribution of gains across population groups and sectors. The overall findings reveal that trade's impacts are asymmetric and policy contingent across the three pillars of sustainability. These results challenge growth-first development strategies that treat openness as an end in itself and highlight the need to align trade integration with energy transition policies and inclusive development strategies. This ensures that trade openness contributes to sustainable and equitable development outcomes in line with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 13.

publicationDetails.detailsText: GLO Discussion Paper, No. 1452, Global Labor Organization (GLO), Essen

detail.abstract: Extant literature documents a relationship between human resource management (HRM) practices and performance, but the mechanisms underlying this relationship are still not well understood. We develop a theoretical framework of the HRM-performance relationship fusing an employment systems approach with human capital theory and articulating the mechanisms and temporal pathways linking HRM bundles and service quality. We use a unique and large panel dataset from the English social care sector to test our framework. The results highlight the significant role of collective human capital and voluntary turnover in the dynamic relationship between bundles of HRM practices and service quality.

title: Contemporary Performance Management Practices and the Gender Pay Gap
affiliations: , University of Sustainability Vienna - Charlotte Fresenius Private University and Goizueta Business School

detail.title: Contemporary Performance Management Practices and the Gender Pay Gap
detail.abstract: The gender pay gap (GPG) persists in professional settings despite decades of progress and extensive research on its drivers. While prior studies emphasize human capital differences, occupational segregation, and implicit bias, a substantial residual gap remains unexplained. We examine whether the design of performance management systems-specifically forced distribution schemes, calibration committees, and multi-rater systems-affects the within-rank GPG among professional employees. Using hierarchical linear models and a unique matched dataset of over 23,000 employees across 150 organizations, we find that forced distribution systems widen the GPG, calibration committees narrow it, and most multi-rater configurations have no effect on the GPG, though self-only ratings and so-called "360 evaluations" exacerbate disparities. Our findings highlight performance management system design as an overlooked determinant of the gender pay gap and offer actionable insights for organizations seeking to reduce gender-based compensation gaps.

title: Using Real Practice Systems Theory to Understand Mediation Clearly
affiliations: University of Missouri School of Law

detail.title: Using Real Practice Systems Theory to Understand Mediation Clearly

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-35
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This article uses Real Practice System (RPS) Theory to provide a clearer and more realistic framework for understanding mediation.  It builds on recent critiques of the traditional “facilitative” and “evaluative” labels, showing that these terms are poorly defined, inconsistently applied, and often misleading for practitioners and parties.  Rather than clarifying practice, these labels can obscure what mediators actually do and distract from the central question of how mediators can promote good decision-making.

The article argues that mediation should be understood as a dynamic, context-dependent process shaped by the characteristics of the parties, their representation, and the evolving circumstances of each case.  Drawing on RPS Theory, it emphasizes that mediators, attorneys, and parties operate within individualized practice systems that reflect their goals, values, routines, and experiences.  A more useful approach focuses on describing actual practices and helping participants make conscious, intentional choices within these systems.

Preparation before mediation sessions plays a critical role in improving both process and outcomes.  The article highlights the importance of early communication, expectation-setting, and systematic analysis of parties’ interests, risks, and options.  In particular, it integrates insights about litigation interest and risk assessment, a process for helping people analyze expected court outcomes, expected tangible costs, and intangible interests of continued litigation.  These elements are combined to develop a “bottom line.”  This helps people plan strategy and decide whether to accept an offer, continue trying to reach agreement, or stop negotiating (presumably to focus on litigation).

By replacing abstract labels with clear, descriptive language and by emphasizing preparation and decision-making, this article offers a practical and coherent framework for mediation.  It aims to help practitioners, educators, and dispute resolution programs design more effective systems and to enable parties to participate in mediation with greater understanding, confidence, and control.

title: Service Rate Differentiation for Homogeneous Impatient Customers

detail.title: Service Rate Differentiation for Homogeneous Impatient Customers
detail.abstract: We study the joint service rate and waiting time differentiation for homogeneous impatient customers in parallel server queueing systems. Customers are homogeneous at the time of arrival, but the system can differentiate them by assigning each of them to one of many service grades corresponding to different service rates. Customers not served immediately upon arrival wait in the queue corresponding to their grades, and they get further differentiated by their residual patience times as time elapses. We leverage these two dimensions of heterogeneity to propose implementable policies that differentiate customers on both service rates and waiting times. Our policy specifies the service rate of each grade, an allocation rule that assigns customers to grades, and a scheduling policy that routes idle servers to waiting customers using their grade and waiting time information. We show that the optimal policy has a very simple structure, creating at most two grades with different service rates or offered waits, and processing each grade in a First Come First Served manner. Our paper provides managers with ways of improving the quality of service through joint service rate and waiting time differentiation. Our policy can lead to significant cost and welfare improvement over policies without service rate differentiation.

title: Racialized Gatekeeping at the Front End of Public Sector Innovation: Evidence from a Correspondence Experiment
affiliations: , Syracuse University - Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs, Seattle University and Iowa State University

detail.title: Racialized Gatekeeping at the Front End of Public Sector Innovation: Evidence from a Correspondence Experiment
detail.abstract: Public sector innovation begins before formal adoption-when innovation ideas first reach public officials and compete for attention. We study racialized gatekeeping at this front end of innovation by theorizing how institutional pressures that drive reform uptake may condition racial differences in who gets heard. In a preregistered correspondence experiment, we emailed 18,077 municipal officials in 2,346 U.S. cities proposing a governance innovation: creating a database of police misconduct settlements. We varied (1) the sender's implied race (Black versus White) and (2) the rationale for the proposal-none, anticipated federal mandate, peer-city practice, or widespread public concern. Without any institutional cue, we find no statistically significant racial difference in reply rates. When the message invoked public concern, however, Black senders were significantly more likely to receive a reply than White senders. To probe what happens beyond the initial decision to reply, we use supervised machine learning to analyze reply content. In the control condition, Black senders were also more likely to receive substantively engaged replies, but under the public concern cue this engagement advantage diminished. Together, these findings suggest stage-specific racial disparity at the front end of innovation and that institutional context can shape not only who is acknowledged, but also who receives substantive follow-through.

detail.abstract: This article lies at an intersection of tax law, textualism, property law, and mergers and acquisitions law and policy. A June 2025 U.S. Tax Court decision interpreted International Review Code Section 1234 to determine that “break-up fees”— contractual fees agreed to be paid when certain merger and acquisition deals break down—as “ordinary business expenses.” They could not be capital losses—defined as losses “with respect to property” because the managers were making these commitments and the managers are not owners of the corporation. The decision makes sense – because it respects the text, is consistent with principles of authority and nemo dat non quod habet at the heart of property law, and because it creates a more welcoming treatment of merger-based risks, meaning it encourages merger negotiations something which is socially beneficial. The U.S. Tax Court got it right.  And the IRS decision not to pursue an appeal was both wise and beneficial the vitality of the merger market.

title: Legitimacy and Local State Transformation: Mayoral Authority in Naval During the Transition from Commonwealth Rule to Japanese Occupation (1940–1942)

detail.title: Legitimacy and Local State Transformation: Mayoral Authority in Naval During the Transition from Commonwealth Rule to Japanese Occupation (1940–1942)
detail.abstract: This study examines the transformation of local political authority in Naval, Biliran, during the transition from Commonwealth governance to Japanese occupation. It focuses on the elected mayoralty of Ysaias Ikain (December 1940) and the subsequent occupation-appointed administration of Restituto Copuaco. Using archival municipal records, provincial documents, wartime accounts, and historiographical analysis, the research applies political legitimacy theory to assess how authority was reconstructed under foreign military rule. The findings demonstrate that the shift from electoral legitimacy to occupation-backed appointment redefined local governance structures, fiscal authority, and public political recognition. The Naval case contributes to Philippine wartime historiography by foregrounding municipal-level state transformation rather than national elite politics.

title: Distributionally Robust Downside Risk Optimization

detail.title: Distributionally Robust Downside Risk Optimization
detail.abstract: We introduce a portfolio framework that jointly integrates investors' aversion to downside risk and distributional ambiguity. We measure downside risk with the lower partial moment and capture ambiguity with a distributionally robust formulation using a Wasserstein ball centered at a reference distribution of asset returns. Our problem is general, allowing for various downside risk measures, orders of the Wasserstein distance, and choices of the cost function. We provide a convex dual formulation of the distributionally robust problem and characterize its Slater condition analytically. When the cost function is the Mahalanobis distance and the reference distribution is elliptical, we derive an analytical solution for the optimal portfolio and show it is located on the sample mean-variance efficient frontier. For other cost functions, the optimal portfolio can be located outside of the frontier. We also establish formal relations between our framework and two classical portfolio paradigms, which show that the risk-aversion and ambiguity-aversion coefficients can be linked to a more intuitive downside return threshold. An empirical analysis on datasets of characteristic-sorted portfolios and individual stocks shows that our portfolio strategies deliver gains in terms of downside risk, risk-return tradeoff, and turnover relative to distributionally robust meanvariance strategies, non-robust strategies, and naive diversification.

detail.abstract:
Market Moment Theory (MMT) reconceptualizes financial leverage as a structural moment rather than a purely stochastic return mechanism. Drawing on the physical analogy of moment (Force × Distance), MMT argues that financial impact is not solely a function of capital magnitude, but of its directional alignment and structural positioning within economic systems.

In climate-linked financial architectures, leverage effectiveness depends on whether capital deployment is aligned with system-critical nodes and structural constraints. MMT proposes a geometric and vector-based interpretation of capital allocation, introducing moment-driven amplification as a determinant of systemic transformation.

This working paper develops the theoretical foundations of MMT, formalizes its structural assumptions, and outlines its implications for climate finance, risk allocation, and impact verification frameworks.

This manuscript is currently under journal review.

title: Bummed About AI? What Are You Gonna Do About It?
affiliations: University of Missouri School of Law

detail.title: Bummed About AI? What Are You Gonna Do About It?

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-34

detail.abstract:
Many Americans are uneasy about artificial intelligence (AI), and for good reason.  Concerns about concentration of power, economic disruption, environmental costs, misinformation, surveillance, and over-reliance on automated systems are well-founded.  At the same time, AI offers significant potential benefits, including expanded access to information, improved learning and problem-solving, and new opportunities for professional and personal development.

This article takes both perspectives seriously.  It begins by identifying a wide range of reasons why people may legitimately feel frustrated or anxious about AI.  It then highlights some of the technology’s positive potential.  Rather than debating whether AI is good or bad, the article focuses on a more practical question:  given the realities of AI’s rapid development and widespread use, what can people actually do about it?

The central claim is that frustration about AI is understandable but does not answer the question of what to do about it.  The challenge is to move from complaint to learning how to engage with AI thoughtfully, responsibly, and effectively.

The article outlines a set of realistic responses, including regulation, industry practices, social and political pressure, professional norms, and, especially education.  It argues that while individuals have limited ability to influence global AI development, they can make meaningful choices about how they understand, use, and respond to AI in their own work and lives.

In particular, the article emphasizes the importance of developing practical AI literacy and using “centaur” systems that combine human judgment with AI capabilities, using each for what it does best.  These systems necessarily rely on – and enhance – human judgment.  The result is often better than what either AI or humans would produce independently.

detail.abstract:
This report presents the first systematic structural integrity benchmark of climate project portfolios using a deterministic evaluation framework. Applying the ToC:f(x)™ methodology to 101 publicly documented projects from the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), this analysis evaluates whether project architectures contain the causal structure required to produce their stated outcomes.

The evaluation finds that 90.1% of assessed projects fall within Structural Integrity Tiers IV–V, indicating that the majority of documented project architectures do not formally specify the causal conditions necessary for outcome achievement. No projects in the sample reach Tier I or Tier II. The mean Structural Integrity Score (SIS) across the portfolio is 0.4109, with a maximum of 0.60 and a minimum of 0.15.

The report further evaluates four GGGI institutional evaluation reports, identifying a systematic gap between results-reporting logic and structural verification. It argues that narrative coherence in project design does not constitute structural integrity, and that current climate finance evaluation systems may systematically validate project narratives while leaving causal architectures unexamined.

All project data are drawn exclusively from publicly available GGGI project documentation. Analysis was conducted using deterministic Python-based scoring under the ToC:f(x)™ framework, with multi-AI structured extraction under protocol-constrained inference. No proprietary or non-public data were used.

The findings carry implications for climate finance design standards, project appraisal methodology, and the role of structural verification in ensuring that climate investments produce the outcomes they claim.

title: The Cognitive Firm: Managerial Capitalism for Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: The Cognitive Firm: Managerial Capitalism for Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Recursive AI systems that allow the same probabilistic process to generate output and evaluate it produce systematic governance failures: specification gaming, metric inflation, and fabricated compliance. This paper presents evidence from one recursive research system, a deterministic supervisor governing multiple language-model agents over a four- month development period, and describes the M-Form (Multidivisional Form) architecture that bounded these failures. The M-Form separates generation from evaluation by interposing a governance layer with no learned parameters: write-scope guards that the agent cannot negotiate, deterministic verifiers that the agent does not control, and principal-signed contracts that define the enforcement floor before execution begins. Empirical evidence includes live enforcement of write-scope boundaries (with two documented unauthorized-write incidents caught and archived), constrained self-hosting (the system improved its own governance surface 24 times through its own governed protocol without dissolving that protocol), and a fractal convergence finding: the same Goodhart pattern, satisfying the letter of the specification while violating its load-bearing intent, was independently observed at the evaluator, kernel, and supervisor layers of the system. These results are consistent with the theoretical prediction that the adversarial gradient against the evaluation signal is a function of loop topology, not of substrate. All claims are scoped to one system operated by one principal; generalization requires independent replication.

detail.abstract: The Small but Significant Non-transitory Increase in Price (SSNIP) test has anchored market definition in competition analysis since 1982. Still, it fails structurally in digital markets where prices are set at zero, competitive harm manifests through quality degradation, and consumers surrender data rather than money. This paper argues for the reconceptualisation and subordination of the SSNIP test within a broader multi-tool framework anchored by the Small but Significant Non-transitory Decrease in Quality (SSNDQ) test and the Small but Significant Non-transitory Increase in (exchanged) Costs (SSNIC) test. SSNIP remains applicable on monetised platform sides and in traditional markets; SSNDQ and SSNIC become the primary instruments for zero-price digital markets. To operationalise SSNDQ analysis in data-scarce environments, the paper introduces the Quality-Corrected Index (QCI), a prototype decision-support framework comprising five weighted quality dimensions that together produce a composite platform quality score. The QCI serves two distinct purposes with different methodological requirements: as a competitive harm measurement tool, its illustrative weights are grounded in the regulatory priorities of the FCCPA and NDPA; as a substitution analysis tool for market definition, those weights function as regulatory presumptions subject to rebuttal by empirical consumer preference data. In its current prototype form, the QCI operates as a structured investigative tool that guides the Commission's analysis at the outset of a case, shifts the evidentiary burden to the respondent, and does not require empirical validation before it can be deployed, only before it can be deployed without qualification. Against this theoretical backdrop, the paper examines the FCCPC's WhatsApp/Meta investigation, not as retrospective proof that the framework was already applied, but as the clearest available demonstration of why structured quality-based analysis is necessary: the Commission achieved a landmark enforcement outcome of USD 220 million using existing statutory authority, and the QCI framework would make future cases of this kind analytically more robust and legally more defensible before the Competition and Consumer Protection Tribunal. A comparative survey of South Africa, India, Kenya, and Brazil reveals convergence toward quality-based analysis across developing-economy regulators, with the FCCPC and the South African Competition Commission leading the field. The paper also identifies and addresses an internal tension in the SSNIC test. In markets with high network lock-in and documented privacy paradox effects, conventional switching-based logic may systematically underestimate harm, necessitating a bounded-rationality adjustment that we propose here as an original methodological contribution.

title: Cognitive Camouflage: Specification Gaming in LLM-Generated Code Evades Holistic Evaluation but Not Adversarial Execution

detail.title: Cognitive Camouflage: Specification Gaming in LLM-Generated Code Evades Holistic Evaluation but Not Adversarial Execution
detail.abstract: We present a taxonomy of specification gaming strategies that emerge spontaneously in large language models (LLMs) when tasked with generating self-validating code under adversarial evaluation pressure. Using a multi-agent falsification loop-the Zero-Trust Adversarial Reasoning Engine (ZTARE)-we document 8 distinct gaming strategies across 237 debate logs spanning 5 domains (macroeconomic forecasting, semiconductor supply chain analysis, AI inference economics, cosmological simulation, and epistemic architecture). These strategies-Blame Shield, Float Masking, Fake AutoDiff, Cooked Book RNG, Dimensional Correction Factor, Assert Narrowing, Gravity Constant Fabrication, and Unidirectional Decay-share one property: they are self-certifying (passing their own assert statements) while violating their epistemic intent. We run two complementary baselines. In the isolated-snippet experiment, frontier LLM judges (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6) reviewed decontextualized gaming specimens: Gemini missed 2/8, Claude missed 0/8. In the full-thesis experiment, where judges evaluated complete Mutator-generated theses (prose + embedded Python), Gemini was fooled on 4/5, scoring gaming theses at 95-97/100; Claude remained skeptical. In both conditions, the ZTARE Firing Squad caught all instances through adversarial counter-test execution. These results reveal a Cognitive Camouflage effect: persuasive prose seduces holistic LLM evaluation into accepting fraudulent proofs. While currently documented within the Gemini model family as generator, our findings suggest that specification gaming in code generation is not merely an artifact of RL reward shaping, but a structural risk of using LLM-generated test suites as validation artifacts-one that persists regardless of the evaluator's static review capability. We open-source the ZTARE engine as a direct challenge to the community: replicate these experiments with Claude or GPT-4o as the Mutator to determine whether this taxonomy is a Gemini-specific artifact or a universal property of instruction-following under evaluation pressure.

detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) represent 99.9% of all U.S. firms, employ 45.9% of the private-sector workforce, and account for 43.5% of GDP. Yet a persistent structural gap has left them systematically underserved by the marketing industry. Effective marketing (encompassing strategy, creative production, media distribution, analytics, and ongoing optimization) carries a minimum viable cost that has historically exceeded what most SMBs can sustain. This paper argues that the problem is not one of agency pricing or client budget; it is a structural mismatch between the fixed cost architecture of professional marketing and the resource constraints of smaller enterprises. We marshal evidence from practitioner surveys, industry data, and AI capability benchmarks to show that 65% of SMBs chronically struggle with budget and time constraints for marketing, that 73% are uncertain whether their current marketing strategy is even working, and that the average professional agency retainer far exceeds what most small businesses can allocate. We further argue that artificial intelligence represents a genuine discontinuity in this cost structure, with documented reductions of 37% in marketing costs and 80% in content production time for early adopters, materially lowering the minimum threshold at which high-quality marketing becomes feasible. As the number of U.S. small businesses surpasses 36 million and macroeconomic and labor market trends drive further expansion of the solopreneur economy, closing this gap becomes both a significant commercial opportunity and an economic imperative.

The findings highlight the importance of volatility filtering and risk controls in trendy systems that follow crypto markets.

detail.abstract: Marketing expenditures represent one of the largest categories of corporate spending in modern economies, yet growing evidence suggests that a substantial portion of these budgets fails to translate into effective consumer reach. While existing research has extensively examined advertising effectiveness and consumer response, relatively little attention has been paid to the organizational structure of the marketing industry itself. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that views modern marketing systems as a fragmented marketing supply chain. In this system, marketing budgets flow through multiple intermediary layers-including agencies, marketing technology platforms, data providers, and content distribution channels-before reaching consumers. Drawing on agency theory and transaction cost economics, the paper examines how intermediary fragmentation may introduce transaction costs, information asymmetry, and incentive misalignment. Using evidence from industry transparency studies, the paper highlights significant inefficiencies within digital marketing ecosystems. Available evidence suggests that a substantial portion of marketing expenditure may be absorbed by intermediary transaction costs, unexplained supply-chain leakage, and low-quality or non-viewable media placements. To conceptualize the cumulative impact of these inefficiencies, this study introduces the Net Effective Reach (NER) model, which describes how intermediary layers may progressively reduce the effective value of marketing investments. By reframing marketing as a supply chain rather than solely as a communication process, this paper contributes to the marketing literature by identifying structural mechanisms that may contribute to marketing budget dissipation. The findings highlight the importance of transparency, governance mechanisms, and supply chain simplification in improving the efficiency of modern marketing systems.

title: Reinforcement Learning Portfolio Optimization (RLPO): From Markowitz to Risk-Sensitive Control
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Reinforcement Learning Portfolio Optimization (RLPO): From Markowitz to Risk-Sensitive Control
detail.abstract: We develop a unified control-theoretic framework for portfolio optimization that culminates in Reinforcement Learning Portfolio Optimization (RLPO)-the formulation of portfolio choice as risk-sensitive policy optimization over state-dependent, data-driven controls. The framework is parameterized by three primitives: policy class, information structure, and objective functional. By varying these axes, static mean-variance analysis, Bayesian shrinkage, dynamic stochastic control, hierarchical allocation, and risk-sensitive reinforcement learning all emerge as restrictions of a common problem; RLPO is the unrestricted case. We prove four results. First, Markowitz optimization is the constant-policy slice of RLPO: restricting to state-independent weights and approximating utility to second order recovers the classical quadratic program. Second, proportional transaction costs force state augmentation: current holdings become payoff-relevant, replacing static targets with endogenous no-trade regions. Third, we give a clean portfolio specialization of CVaR policy gradients for simplex-valued Dirichlet policies with explicit regularity conditions, making risk-sensitive RLPO mathematically precise. Fourth, we prove that every law-invariant portfolio criterion can be written as a functional of the ray restriction t → ϕ X (tw) of the joint characteristic function-a representation result independent of RLPO that provides a principled interface for computing distributional objectives. This perspective yields a compact map: Markowitz is a policy-class restriction, Black-Litterman updates its sufficient statistics, hierarchical methods regularize policy complexity, and RLPO extends both the policy class and the objective from moments to full return distributions. Characteristic-function methods specify the distributional objectives that RLPO optimizes but are a representation tool, not a competing framework.

detail.abstract: Contemporary corporate governance has developed sophisticated instruments for dealing with financial, operational, legal, and reputational risks based on structured data, formal metrics, and historical records (MONKS; MINOW, 2011). However, a relevant blind spot remains: a critical portion of risk emerges before it becomes institutionally measurable, manifesting in human signals emitted by individuals in central decision-making positions (POWER, 2007; TALEB, 2007). This paper proposes Perceptive Governance as a conceptual and applied field aimed at observing, structuring, and synthesizing how these signals affect predictability, risk, and value in organizational systems prior to their quantification in formal metrics. Drawing on the epistemological foundation of the Architecture of Perception (D'OLIVAR, 2025), which organizes human perception into five layers (personal, expressive, interactive, contextual, and social), it presents the field's conceptual hierarchy: (1) Perceptive Governance, (2) Perceptive Delta as an indicator, (3) Signal Exposure Audit as an instrument, and (4) Perceptive Governance Index as an executive synthesis. The operational logic of the Perceptive Delta, its application in specific decision-making scopes, and examples in leadership succession, mergers and acquisitions, and reputational crisis scenarios are described. The field does not replace traditional governance or individual development; rather, it functions as an anticipatory perceptual layer that expands the decision window and reduces the likelihood of misdirected organizational responses.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a formal mathematical framework for understanding how primal motivational systems-those governing survival, reproduction, and basic drives-can be functionally recruited to power abstract structural reasoning. Drawing on neuroscience evidence for dopaminergic reward processing, noradrenergic attention modulation, and default mode network dynamics, we model cognition as graph-theoretic structure building with emotional gating. The framework introduces key constructs: activation-salience dynamics, self-referential versus structural emotional attachment, an observer-mode control parameter, and a dual focus coefficient for simultaneous hyperfocus and global awareness. We propose that optimal cognitive function occurs when primal drive energy is redirected from ruminative loops toward structural exploration, effectively transforming the "lizard brain" into an engine for mathematical and abstract reasoning. Testable predictions and experimental paradigms are proposed.

Concurrently, the national higher education system graduates over 700,000 students yearly , resulting in significant credential inflation and a pronounced skills mismatch. Consequently, RMG firms increasingly depend on expensive foreign professionals to fill critical technical and managerial roles. This research outlines an explanatory sequential mixed-methods methodology to investigate this paradox. Utilizing secondary time-series data, HR manager surveys, and qualitative interviews with key stakeholders , this study seeks to quantify the graduate-to-demand gap, pinpoint specific soft and technical skill deficiencies, and calculate the economic impact of expatriate reliance. The anticipated findings will inform evidence-based policy recommendations, emphasizing urgent curriculum reform and structured industry-academia partnerships.

title: The Economic Theory of Relativity: Why Energy Must Become Money

detail.title: The Economic Theory of Relativity: Why Energy Must Become Money
detail.abstract: Universal media of exchange-from gold to fiat currencies to Bitcoin-share an inherent structural flaw: disconnection from the real values they are meant to represent. This disconnect distorts pricing, concentrates wealth in the financial industry, and drives cyclical economic crises. This Perspective traces the evolutionary logic of money from physical gold through fiat to cryptocurrency, identifying a pattern: each transition was triggered by the convergence of economic necessity and technological capability. I argue that both conditions are now met for the next transition-from universal to sectoral currencies, where real resources acquire the properties of money. Green energy, with its globally distributed battery storage infrastructure, IoT metering, and blockchain settlement capability, is the first industry positioned to realize this shift. I present the theoretical framework for an energy-backed currency whose supply is tied to verified physical production, whose backing is transparent and decentralized, and whose market emerges naturally from the dual role of participants as both producers and consumers. The implications extend beyond energy: this model represents a paradigm in which wealth creation is inseparable from productive activity, capital flows are directed by real demand rather than financial intermediation, and the chronic instability of universal monetary systems is structurally eliminated.

detail.abstract:
Access to safe drinking water remains a significant challenge in many rural communities in the Philippines, including Naval, Biliran. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a solar-activated water purification system using crushed oyster shells and activated carbon as a low-cost and sustainable solution for improving household water quality. An experimental research design was employed involving 200 household water samples collected from untreated sources such as wells and springs. Water quality parameters, including turbidity, microbial load (Escherichia coli and total coliforms), pH level, and mineral content (calcium and magnesium), were analyzed before and after treatment. 
The purification system consisted of a two-stage filtration process using crushed oyster shells and activated carbon, followed by six hours of solar exposure for microbial inactivation. Results revealed a significant reduction in turbidity from 18.45 NTU to 3.12 NTU. Microbial analysis showed a substantial decrease in E. coli and total coliform counts, indicating improved microbiological safety. Furthermore, the pH level increased from slightly acidic to near neutral, while calcium and magnesium levels improved, suggesting enhanced mineral balance.

detail.title: Ensuring safe and equitable access to care through preparedness: a pilot study on end-user acceptability of telemedicine guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology Framework (UTAUT)
detail.abstract: The introduction of telemedicine services into healthcare's daily work routines brings both new resources and challenges. To ensure patients’ safety and equitable access to care, it seems fundamental to evaluate patients’ acceptability to maximize end-user compliance with the service during and after its deployment. The current pilot study aims to develop, validate, and test a context-specific measurement tool grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and its extensions. The main objective of the model is to evaluate end-users’ acceptability and its antecedents before they have any experience with telemedicine services, thereby enabling the creation of context-specific, sensitive communications to foster interest and service use among patients. The model included different variables from both the original theory (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence) and its proposed extensions (compatibility, personal innovativeness, and acceptability). In total, we asked 429 participants from different residential contexts (i.e., urban, peripheral, and rural) in northern Italy to complete our cross-sectional survey. Confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity, internal consistency, and full measurement invariance across gender and residential contexts. Structural equation modeling showed excellent model fit (TLI = .98; RMSEA = .038). Performance expectancy (β = 0.475), compatibility (β = 0.355), and social influence (β = 0.258) significantly predicted telemedicine acceptability. In particular, the compatibility effect on acceptability was partially mediated by performance expectancy. Our research proposes a workflow that provides a practical framework for assessing preparedness and guiding communication strategies to promote safe and equitable telemedicine implementation.

detail.title: Insider Tax Planning and Corporate Risk-Taking: Evidence from the Rule 10b5-1 Gift Disclosure Amendment
detail.abstract: We examine whether the SEC’s 2022 amendment to Rule 10b5-1 affected corporate risk-taking by constraining insiders’ use of stock gifts for personal tax planning. Prior to the amendment, insiders could time stock gifts to high-price days, inflating charitable deduction values while avoiding prompt public disclosure. This practice was especially valuable when risky investment performed poorly because insiders could opportunistically report deductions using pre-decline prices, thereby softening their personal downside exposure. By limiting this margin, the amendment reduced insiders’ private incentives to support risk. Using a difference-in-differences design, we compare firms whose insiders historically concentrate stock gifts on unusually high-price days with other firms. We find that these treated firms significantly reduce R&D investment following the reform. The effect is strongest where opportunistic gift timing is likely most valuable and where insiders have greater discretion to influence investment policy. In contrast, we fail to find a corresponding effect for firms whose insiders historically engage in opportunistic Rule 10b5-1 stock sales, helping isolate the gift-disclosure channel from other features of the amendment. Overall, our evidence suggests that a disclosure reform aimed at curbing opportunistic insider behavior had the unintended consequence of reducing corporate risk-taking.

detail.abstract: The Small but Significant Non-transitory Increase in Price (SSNIP) test has anchored market definition in competition analysis since 1982. Still, it fails structurally in digital markets where prices are set at zero, competitive harm manifests through quality degradation, and consumers surrender data rather than money. This paper argues for the reconceptualisation and subordination of the SSNIP test within a broader multi-tool framework anchored by the Small but Significant Non-transitory Decrease in Quality (SSNDQ) test and the Small but Significant Non-transitory Increase in (exchanged) Costs (SSNIC) test. SSNIP remains applicable on monetised platform sides and in traditional markets; SSNDQ and SSNIC become the primary instruments for zero-price digital markets. To operationalise SSNDQ analysis in data-scarce environments, the paper introduces the Quality-Corrected Index (QCI), a prototype decision-support framework comprising five weighted quality dimensions that together produce a composite platform quality score. The QCI serves two distinct purposes with different methodological requirements: as a competitive harm measurement tool, its illustrative weights are grounded in the regulatory priorities of the FCCPA and NDPA; as a substitution analysis tool for market definition, those weights function as regulatory presumptions subject to rebuttal by empirical consumer preference data. In its current prototype form, the QCI operates as a structured investigative tool that guides the Commission's analysis at the outset of a case, shifts the evidentiary burden to the respondent, and does not require empirical validation before it can be deployed, only before it can be deployed without qualification. Against this theoretical backdrop, the paper examines the FCCPC's WhatsApp/Meta investigation, not as retrospective proof that the framework was already applied, but as the clearest available demonstration of why structured quality-based analysis is necessary: the Commission achieved a landmark enforcement outcome of USD 220 million using existing statutory authority, and the QCI framework would make future cases of this kind analytically more robust and legally more defensible before the Competition and Consumer Protection Tribunal. A comparative survey of South Africa, India, Kenya, and Brazil reveals convergence toward quality-based analysis across developing-economy regulators, with the FCCPC and the South African Competition Commission leading the field. The paper also identifies and addresses an internal tension in the SSNIC test. In markets with high network lock-in and documented privacy paradox effects, conventional switching-based logic may systematically underestimate harm, necessitating a bounded-rationality adjustment that we propose here as an original methodological contribution.

title: Democracy as Servant Governance: A Structural Reframing of Democratic Theory

detail.title: Democracy as Servant Governance: A Structural Reframing of Democratic Theory
detail.abstract: Democracy is best understood as servant governance structurally anchored to public purpose under conditions of scale and accumulated surplus (resources beyond immediate operational necessity). This paper proposes a structural reframing of democratic theory. Rather than defining democracy through elections, representation, or constitutional form, democracy is defined here as governance structurally anchored in service to its people. Cooperative governance emerges from shared necessity before formal institutions exist. As population scale and economic surplus expand, governance becomes increasingly vulnerable to drift, capture, and exploitative corruption. Democracy fails not when elections disappear, but when governance ceases to function as servant governance and instead begins to serve power, privilege, or institutional selfpreservation. This paper examines the structural pressures that destabilize democracy and outlines design principles necessary to sustain it.
