title:
The Prompt Expertise Externality: 
AI Adoption, Human Capital, and the Dynamic Productivity Trap

detail.title:
The Prompt Expertise Externality: 
AI Adoption, Human Capital, and the Dynamic Productivity Trap
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a formal dynamic model of a novel market failure arising from rapid AI
adoption: the destruction of human capital required to effectively use AI, which I term prompt
expertise. I distinguish two channels through which professional workers accumulate the prompt
expertise required to direct AI systems. The active channel — learning by performing analytical
tasks — may partially survive automation. The passive channel — learning by observing
consequential decisions, institutional dynamics, and the gap between formal analysis and real-
world outcomes — requires employment in professional environments and cannot be replicated
by training programs or task performance alone. Because passive expertise constitutes general
rather than firm-specific human capital, competitive firms lack incentive to preserve entry-level
employment. I formalize this market failure, show that aggregate output is non-monotone in AI
adoption speed, with an interior maximum below the competitive equilibrium rate, and derive
conditions under which the competitive equilibrium overshoots the socially optimal adoption rate.
The active/passive distinction sharpens both the theoretical mechanism and the policy response:
interventions that preserve employment, not merely task performance, are required to sustain the
passive accumulation channel.

title: A Fixed-Friction Clearing Model of Time-Inconsistent Behavior: Reevaluating Procrastination under Biological Shadow Debt

detail.title: A Fixed-Friction Clearing Model of Time-Inconsistent Behavior: Reevaluating Procrastination under Biological Shadow Debt
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Fixed-Friction Clearing Model, an interdisciplinary framework synthesizing neurobiological allostatic load with (S, s) inventory control theory to reconstruct the micro-foundations of time-inconsistent behavior. Challenging the conventional "irrationality hypothesis" in behavioral economics, we demonstrate that intertemporal decision-making is fundamentally a Local Optimal Stopping Problem constrained by a relative fixed friction cost (C) and cumulative generalized shadow debt (D(t)). The model delineates a deterministic tri-state phase transition mechanism: (1) Temporary Stasis (procrastination) as an energy-minimizing local optimum when D(t) < C; (2) Pulse Clearing as a forced physical jump triggered by a systemic "margin call" when D(t) >= C; and (3) Rational Abandonment as a global stop-loss strategy when physical barriers exceed physiological capacity (C > D_max). Furthermore, this topological structure provides an endogenous physical mapping for Loss Aversion (asymmetrical margin constraints) and Scarcity Myopia (time horizon collapse due to high baseline debt). We conclude that observed behavioral anomalies are not cognitive defects but inevitable mechanical outcomes of a precision state machine operating under strict physical boundary conditions.

title: From attitudes to action: Factors influencing implementation of evidence-based practice in Australian community and outpatient substance use treatment setting

detail.title: From attitudes to action: Factors influencing implementation of evidence-based practice in Australian community and outpatient substance use treatment setting
detail.abstract: IntroductionImplementing evidence-based practice (EBP) is a key goal across all healthcare settings, including in substance use treatment settings. However, limited research has explored clinician’s perceptions about EBP, their intentions to use EBP, and the barriers they face in substance use treatment settings.MethodsUsing a cross-sectional design, clinicians from 31 community-based substance use treatment centres across Australia completed a self-report survey which included the Evidence-Based Practice Inventory (EBPI) and items regarding staff characteristics (e.g., age, gender, professional role). A key informant at each centre also completed a survey to provide information about the centre’s organizational characteristics (e.g., government or non-government, client load). Regression analysis was used to examine the staff and centre characteristics associated with positive perceptions of evidence-based practice.ResultsAmong the 213 clinicians surveyed, the highest EBPI scores were found in the attitude domain, where over 80% of participants expressing positive attitudes towards EBP. Lower scores were reported for the decision-making and intention and behaviour domains. At the individual staff level, older age was associated with lower overall EBPI scores (mean score difference range -6.28 to -9.62. p=0.002). At the organisational level, being a non-government treatment centre was positively associated with the overall EBPI scores when compared to government centres (mean score difference 8.66, p=0.021).ConclusionsAlthough clinicians generally hold positive attitudes towards EBP, their intention to implement in clinical practice is low. Further research is needed to better understand the factors that influence the implementation of EBP implementation in the substance use setting.

title: Cluster Strength as a Moderator of Porter's Five Forces: A Conceptual Model and Empirical Agenda

detail.title: Cluster Strength as a Moderator of Porter's Five Forces: A Conceptual Model and Empirical Agenda
detail.abstract: Porter's Five Forces and cluster theory are often treated as separate tools in strategy, even though they address closely related questions. Five Forces explains why some industries are more attractive than others, while cluster theory explains why firms in some locations outperform otherwise similar firms elsewhere. This paper brings those perspectives together by developing the Cluster-Moderated Industry Attractiveness (CMIA) model. The central argument is that regional cluster strength does not merely provide background context; it alters the intensity of the competitive forces themselves. Drawing on Marshallian mechanisms input-output linkages, labor pooling, and knowledge spillovers the model suggests that stronger clusters are likely to reduce supplier power, intensify rivalry, and shape entry conditions in a nonlinear way, while the effects on buyer power and substitution are more context-dependent. The paper does not attempt to settle these relationships empirically. Instead, it develops a conceptual framework, translates that logic into a testable model, and outlines an empirical strategy using data from the U.S. Cluster Mapping Project together with firm-level and patent data. In doing so, it offers a more geographically grounded way to think about industry attractiveness.

detail.abstract: This report analyzes why blockchain innovation has struggled to achieve sustained real-world impact and proposes a methodological response based on participatory, context-sensitive design. Drawing on the Argentina Onchain Residency, which took place in November 2025, it introduces “Participatory Unblocking of Blockchain Use Cases,” an approach that inverts conventional innovation logic by starting from concrete coordination problems and adoption barriers rather than predefined technological solutions. The study brings together insights from over 50 blockchain builders and a wide range of Argentine stakeholders across government, industry, academia, and civil society. It identifies structural, regulatory, and cultural constraints that have limited adoption beyond crypto-native domains, emphasizing the role of institutional misalignment rather than purely technical limitations. Applying a six-step methodology combining problem discovery, contextualization, and collaborative prototyping, the residency generated 21 problem statements and seven functional prototypes across sectors such as public procurement, identity, governance, and local economic coordination. The findings suggest that blockchain’s impact depends less on technical feasibility than on alignment with real-world institutional environments. Participatory, problem-driven design can narrow the gap between blockchain’s promise and utility, provided that incentive structures, stakeholder coordination, and implementation pathways are explicitly addressed.

title: Reconstruction-induced Land and Property Restitution in Postwar Syria: The Problem with Sanctions

detail.title: Reconstruction-induced Land and Property Restitution in Postwar Syria: The Problem with Sanctions
detail.abstract: With the war in Syria appearing to draw to a close—although not along the lines preferred by the West—the realities of what reconstruction will look like and how it will affect the postwar order become primary considerations. As the nearly 13 million forcibly dislocated persons—along with the countries and communities that host them—contemplate possible returns to housing, lands and properties (HLP) within Syria, postwar reconstruction, return migration and restitution emerge as strongly linked. Dislocated populations will not consider returning to areas of origin in significant numbers without reconstruction and the recovery of livelihood opportunities that reconstruction provides. As long as large parts of the country continue to be uninhabitable, the 1 dislocation crises in neighbouring countries, Europe and across Syria will continue. While it is 2 in the West’s interest to encourage returns to areas of origin and restitution of HLP in the  interests of fair, just and secure recovery of livelihoods and overall stability, at the same time Western sanctions on reconstruction actively thwart such a process, particularly in government held areas, which is most of the country. For European and Middle Eastern countries most affected by the presence of large numbers of refugees, this is a fundamentally fraught but important deliberation. Migration and refugee return will be at the center of these discussions. Faced with a lack of reconstruction and the resulting deficit of livelihood and economic opportunities, refugees will not willingly return; and with the surrounding states resisting their integration, many may decide to move on to Europe. And while fewer returns would mean less 3 pressure on the Syrian government to attend to the needs of the overall population, including for HLP restitution, the reverse is also true—effective reconstruction, safely drawing back 4 significant numbers of refugees and IDPs (internally dislocated persons) would pressure the government to meet the restitution and livelihood recovery needs of its postwar population.

title: Myth of Competition in the Dual Banking System

detail.title: Myth of Competition in the Dual Banking System

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The American banking system operates under a dual state and federal system of chartering and safety and soundness regulation. The dual banking system ostensibly allows banks operating in any state to choose between two different sets of primary laws to define their powers and to regulate their activities and investments. Banks may obtain a national charter and fall under the regulatory aegis of the Comptroller of the Currency, or they may obtain a state charter from the chartering state's primary banking regulator and fall under its regulatory aegis. In addition, within this system state banks can further decide whether to subject themselves to federal regulation by becoming members of the Federal Reserve System (Fed) or by insuring deposits through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).

The ideal of the dual banking system, with its overlapping system of state and federal regulation, is perhaps unique in the support it enjoys in the political and scholarly communities. Principal proponents of the economic approach to legal problems regard it as a promising source of efficient legal rules. This efficiency results from competition among state and federal regulators who desire to increase their market share by attracting additional chartering business. Thus, the currently accepted theory posits that competition among state and federal regulators manifests itself in the maximum freedom from regulation consistent with a safe and sound banking system.

At the same time, there is such widespread political support among regulators and politicians for the dual banking system that “questioning the underlying premise of the dual banking system has traditionally been outside the borders of permissible political discourse.” Indeed, the dual banking system “has long been a sacred cow in the American political tradition.”

The thesis of this Article, however, is that the efficiency justifications for the dual banking system are entirely misplaced. We find that the substantive differences between federal and state chartering regulations are far more apparent than real. Federal preemption and uniformity, rather than competition and diversity, are the legal norms in banking regulation.

title: The Priority Dilemma of Western Sanctions on Syria's Agricultural Reconstruction Unruh J (forthcoming) The priority dilemma of Western sanctions on Syria's agricultural reconstruction. Journal of Intervention and Statebuilding

detail.title: The Priority Dilemma of Western Sanctions on Syria's Agricultural Reconstruction Unruh J (forthcoming) The priority dilemma of Western sanctions on Syria's agricultural reconstruction. Journal of Intervention and Statebuilding
detail.abstract: The current relationship between Syria and the West cripples any real prospect for reconstruction. Western sanctions on reconstruction as a political tool seeking regime transition or concessions are aimed at accountability, influencing the direction of the war, and protecting civilians. In reality however they have wide-ranging negative impacts on the civilian population both within Syria and in exile-while having little hope of success. For agriculture the repercussions of Western sanctions on reconstruction are particularly severe, affecting refugee returns, livelihood recovery, food security and stabilization. This article examines the priority dilemma of Western sanctions on agricultural reconstruction, and argues that they are counterproductive, particularly given that the war is now larger and more problematic than what a reformed government's relationship with civil society could resolve.

title: The Role of Off-Farm Employment in Tropical Forest Conservation: Labor, Migration, and Smallholder Attitudes Toward Land in Western Uganda

detail.title: The Role of Off-Farm Employment in Tropical Forest Conservation: Labor, Migration, and Smallholder Attitudes Toward Land in Western Uganda
detail.abstract: The potential for off-farm employment (OFE) to contribute significantly to forest conservation in the tropics is a widely held logic among donors, governments, and social scientists. While an aggregate level examination of OFE cases can support this logic, there is disagreement as to the operative aspects of specific linkages and assumptions. This study examines the case of the tea industry in western Uganda, and uses a combination of fieldwork and remote sensing to pursue a more nuanced examination of the role of migration and non-monetary aspects of OFE on forest conservation in both a national park and unprotected forest contexts. Results indicate that the tea industry does serve as an off-farm employer to a limited number of local smallholders but these benefits are offset by the industry's overwhelming dependence on migrant labor which sees OFE as temporary, then seeks to settle locally. There is also evidence that the tea industry is contributing to conservation efforts of Kibale National Park by unintentionally serving as a physical buffer zone, which inhibits both human encroachment on the park and wildlife encroachment on smallholder crops. The latter represents a site-specific phenomenon that holds much potential for future management plans of the area and exemplifies the importance of considering the sitespecific circumstances associated with off-farm employment development.

title: Monasteries as Economic Organizations An Integrative Review of Business Models, Organizational Longevity, and Monastic Management

detail.title: Monasteries as Economic Organizations An Integrative Review of Business Models, Organizational Longevity, and Monastic Management
detail.abstract: Business model research has theorized mission as a contextual antecedent but not as an explicit architectural element of the business model. This article develops the Mission Layer, a construct designating a codified founding mission that operates as a superordinate constraint across the core dimensions of the business model, and examines its implications for business model innovation in identity-anchored organizations. An integrative literature review synthesizes three fragmented streams: monastic management research, business model scholarship, and organizational longevity research. The design accommodates the historical depth and cross-disciplinary synthesis the research problem requires. The synthesis reveals that existing frameworks lack a construct for organizations in which a codified founding mission operates as an operative architectural filter, screening strategic opportunities and excluding options that violate normative constraints. Whereas organizational identity, institutional logic, and imprinting illuminate normative orientation at different levels of analysis, the Mission Layer specifies how such constraints are enacted at the level of business model architecture. Three scope conditions define its applicability: the mission is codified in an institutionally binding document; governance structures reinforce normative compliance across generations; and economic activity operates under mission primacy.Three contributions follow. First, the Mission Layer addresses the absence of a business-model-architectural mechanism for capturing how normative constraints shape innovation. Second, in organizations meeting the scope conditions, normative architectural stability and operational innovation are not mutually exclusive. Third, management history is established as a productive source of theoretical insight for business model research. The construct is derived from monastic evidence; transfer to non-monastic settings requires empirical validation.

detail.abstract: International supporters of Ukraine are increasingly reluctant to fund the war against Russia let alone what will undoubtedly be a massive reconstruction effort for the country — the amount now increasing into the hundreds of billions to possibly over a trillion dollars. With the ongoing targeting of civilian residential areas and critical infrastructure by Russian forces, and almost certain refusal by Western taxpayers to fund the total costs of reconstruction, alternative ways must be found. This includes efforts to identify multinational approaches to raise the necessary military and reconstruction funds.

title: Driving Transformation in War-Related Housing, Land and Property Restitution: Innovations from the Ukraine -Russian War

detail.title: Driving Transformation in War-Related Housing, Land and Property Restitution: Innovations from the Ukraine -Russian War
detail.abstract: Large-scale housing, land and property (HLP) restitution efforts for war-displaced populations face ongoing limitations in three key areas: legal frameworks, financing, and technology. These limitations have led to critical problems in managing population return, reconstruction and political and economic recovery; with particular concern on the emergence of exploitive agendas and social unrest. Ukraine's unfortunate war however presents the opportunity to examine significant advances in mitigating these limitations. Drawing on fieldwork in Ukraine and the author's experience in 23 war-affected countries, the article describes, 1) the socio-legal context and legislative timing of Ukraine's new Compensation Law; 2) the sources, monetization of HLP claims and remedies involved in financing restitution programmes; and 3) the restitution processing speed and social inclusion possible with Ukraine's approach to use of technology.

title: Integrating Remote Sensing Data And Rapid Appraisals For Land-Cover Change Analyses In Uganda
affiliations: Indiana University, Makerere University, , Indiana University, Makerere University, Makerere University and Indiana University

detail.title: Integrating Remote Sensing Data And Rapid Appraisals For Land-Cover Change Analyses In Uganda
detail.abstract: Rapid population growth, unsustainable land use, and a pervasively degrading landscape are components of a dominant paradigm regarding African development. While recent work articulating the 'misreading' of the African landscape have begun to challenge this paradigm, much work remains regarding the pervasiveness and character of this misread. Here we argue that instead of one or two pervasively operating mechanisms resulting in woody biomass change across African landscapes, there may be several mechanisms of human-environment interactions operating simultaneously. Here we present a more rapid method, of use to development practitioners, subnational planners, and scientists, for identifying patterns woody biomass change and characterizing the prevailing mechanisms in a way less influenced by dominant paradigms. We combine remotely sensed products, collected at multiple spatial scales, archival data, and rapid rural appraisals to describe alternative mechanisms of woody biomass accumulation (both forest and tree-cover) in south-central Uganda than those currently understood.

title: The Architecture Of Post-Human Markets

detail.title: The Architecture Of Post-Human Markets
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Reflexivity Tensor Field (RTF), a computable operator for measuring systemic fragility in multi-agent state spaces. It applies to financial markets, where autonomous artificial intelligence agents constitute the dominant participants in price discovery, liquidity provision, and information processing. The RTF is situated within a proposed axiomatic structure for Algorithmic Behavioural Finance comprising four foundational axioms: non-human reflexivity, synthetic epistemology, reputation as collateral, and emergent fragility. The central theoretical prediction concerns asymmetric stress-regime fragility: markets populated by agents with correlated policy parameters are predicted to experience significantly faster liquidity withdrawal and greater spread deterioration during stress events than markets with heterogeneous policies. A Monte Carlo agent-based simulation using parameterised heuristic agents (N = 50, 200 runs, untuned parameters) provides partial computational support: four of five directional predictions are confirmed, including 19.7% agent withdrawal in correlated-policy markets versus 9.8% in heterogeneous-policy markets (p < 10-66), 1.84x spread deterioration versus 0.89x in heterogeneous markets.

title: Single-Asset Adaptive Leveraged Volatility Control

detail.title: Single-Asset Adaptive Leveraged Volatility Control
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a methodology for constructing a market index composed of a liquid risky asset and a liquid risk-free asset that achieves a fixed target volatility. Existing volatility-targeting strategies typically scale portfolio exposure inversely with a variance forecast, but such open-loop approaches suffer from high turnover, leverage spikes, and sensitivity to estimation error---issues that limit practical adoption in index construction. We propose a proportional-control approach for setting the index weights that explicitly corrects tracking error through feedback. The method requires only a few interpretable parameters, making it transparent and practical for index construction. We demonstrate in simulation that this approach is more effective at consistently achieving the target volatility than the open-loop alternative.

title: Assessing Implementation of Current Expected Credit Loss (CECL) using Bank Deposit Interest Rates
affiliations: , Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business and

detail.title: Assessing Implementation of Current Expected Credit Loss (CECL) using Bank Deposit Interest Rates
detail.abstract: CECL framework requires banks to set aside provisions in line with their subjective views about the long-run future credit quality of their loans. Providing empirical evidence on whether and to what extent they do so is challenging because it is impossible to observe banks' information at the time of deciding the provisions. This study proposes using banks' contemporaneous real actions to corroborate banks' decision to use information in provisions. Of all real actions, we argue and find evidence that deposit rates are a suitable proxy for banks' information about long-term economic conditions and future charge-offs, as rates serve as a market-based price of capital and clearly reflects banks' information. Though deposit rates exhibit stronger co-movement with provisions post-CECL adoption, banks do not fully incorporate all the information they have for setting deposit rates in estimating provisions. We propose a timeliness metric using deposit rates. Using this metric and employing spatial identification across U.S. states, we provide novel evidence that while adopting CECL in itself does not mitigate procyclicality banks that are timely can mitigate these effects. Thus, it is not only adoption but also implementation of CECL that collectively determines procyclicality.

title: Socio-Legal Instabilities in Ukraine's Wartime Compensation Law for Damaged and Destroyed Residential Property

detail.title: Socio-Legal Instabilities in Ukraine's Wartime Compensation Law for Damaged and Destroyed Residential Property
detail.abstract: Laws seeking to resolve war-related problems face a significant dilemma. While the legal establishment in a war-affected country drafts laws based on normative approaches suited to peacetime and stable settings, the civilian population pursues crises livelihoods markedly unsuited to compliance with or use of such laws. What emerges are socio-legal instabilities that aggravate instead of resolve wartime problems. With a socio-legal examination of Ukraine's wartime housing Compensation Law, this article describes six sets of instabilities that compromise the utility of the law and aggravate or create additional problems, 1) the case-bycase approach, 2) administrative and institutional capacities, 3) legal vs. available evidence, 4) the time-frame for claims submission and awareness raising, 5) excluded segments of civil society, and 6) prohibitions on selling properties. Approaches from international best practice which may be able to attend to these instabilities are then suggested.

title: Supervised Fine-tuning of Large Language Models on Financial Statements to Predict Future Earnings Changes
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Accounting and

detail.title: Supervised Fine-tuning of Large Language Models on Financial Statements to Predict Future Earnings Changes
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained to recognize patterns in large amounts of text for next-token prediction, and, by doing so, are expected to perform well on general tasks. Recent accounting work demonstrates that the predictive ability of these models for future earnings is entirely attributable to look-ahead bias. We fine-tune an open-source LLM to predict the direction of one-year-ahead earnings changes based on standardized, anonymized financial statements paired with next year’s realized earnings change directions. Our model shows significant out-of-sample predictive power in the period after the LLM’s release date (i.e., free of look-ahead bias), with an area under the Receiver Operating Characteristics curve (AUC) of 68.94 percent. It outperforms a random guess and gradient boosted decision trees trained on the same financial statement items. Analyses suggest that the predictive power comes primarily from the LLM’s prior knowledge, rather than just its complex architecture, particularly in its understanding of the temporal structure and accounting terms in financial statements, which tabular machine learning models often miss. Lastly, a hedge portfolio formed based on the prediction of our model yields annual size-adjusted returns of 10.6 percent. The findings suggest that properly fine-tuned LLMs are powerful tools for earnings forecasting.

title: Negative Vote Eliminates Strategic Voting

detail.title: Negative Vote Eliminates Strategic Voting
detail.abstract: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite Theorem is widely understood to establish that strategic voting is an unavoidable feature of any non-dictatorial voting system with three or more candidates. This paper argues that the theorem's sincerity criterion, developed exclusively in the context of systems offering only positive voting options, is inapplicable to bipolar ballot systems. The Negative Vote (also known as the Balanced Ballot)-in which each voter casts either +1 for a preferred candidate or-1 against a most-opposed candidate-exposes a foundational gap in the standard definition of strategic voting: a vote cast against a candidate is no less sincere than a vote cast in favor. Once this is recognized, the strategic dilemma that drives lesser-evil voting under plurality, ranked-choice, and approval systems dissolves. Under Negative Vote, every available voting action corresponds to a sincere expression of preference; no voter gains by misrepresenting their views. We develop this argument through conceptual analysis, familiar analogues from legislative and judicial voting practice, and comparative examples across major electoral systems.

title: Allocation of Errors and the Architecture of Liability
affiliations: Ghent University - Faculty of Law and Israel Supreme Court

detail.title: Allocation of Errors and the Architecture of Liability

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cardozo Legal Studies Research Paper No. 417
publicationDetails.journalName: Cardozo Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Our civil liability system affords numerous defenses against every single violation of the law. A successful assertion of one of the many defenses by a defendant guarantees her a victory in court.  This architecture of civil liability is fundamentally incompatible with the fact that courts are not immune from errors. When a court erroneously strikes out a meritorious defense, it might still keep the defendant out of harm’s way by granting him another defense. A rightful plaintiff, for her part, must convince the court to deny each and every defense asserted by the defendant. By erroneously granting the defendant one defense out of many, the court will doom the plaintiff’s meritorious suit. Any rate of adjudicative errors — random and completely unbiased — increases the prospect of losing the case for meritorious plaintiffs while decreasing it for defendants, both rightful and opportunistic.

This profound inequality forces plaintiffs to settle suits below their expected value. Worse yet, under the current system, defendants can unilaterally reduce the suit’s expected value and extort a cheap settlement from the plaintiff through a frivolous addition of defenses.

We offer three alternative solutions to this problem: a procedural solution, a compensatory solution, and a substantive solution. Each of our proposed solutions would eradicate the defendants’ anomalous advantage. Our procedural solution would limit defendants to one line of defense against each claim asserted by the plaintiff. Our compensatory solution introduces a damage multiplier for defendants who lose the case. This multiplier increases the compensation duty for liable defendants in proportion to the number of defenses they choose to raise. Our substantive solution replaces the violation/defenses architecture by a comprehensive comparative fault regime, authorizing courts to apportion parties’ responsibility on a scale of 0% to 100%. Under this regime, each party would be free to assert and develop any number of claims about how her fault measures against her opponent’s fault. We show that this solution dominates the other two in tort and contracts cases where individuals’ entitlements and obligations are bilateral, fault-based, and monetized. For differently structured obligations and entitlements, we recommend the procedural and compensatory solutions.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a critical evaluation of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), focusing on its legal authority and the differing treatment of nuclear and non-nuclear states. It analyzes specific NPT articles and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Safeguard Agreements, considering challenges in nuclear governance such as issues with Iran, the AUKUS trilateral security pact, and various working papers from the 2026 NPT review cycle. The paper supports the European Union's urging of the Conference on Disarmament (CD) to begin negotiations for a Fissile Material Cut Off Treaty (FMCT), emphasizing its importance for reinforcing global nuclear non-proliferation. It proposes a strategic shift from the Conference on Disarmament to a United Nations (UN) General Assembly mandate, drawing comparisons with the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). The paper concludes with practical considerations meant to strengthen the international nuclear non-proliferation regime.

title: Understanding the Law of Evidence Through the Lens of Signal-to-Noise
affiliations: Israel Supreme Court

detail.title: Understanding the Law of Evidence Through the Lens of Signal-to-Noise

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cardozo Legal Studies Faculty Research Paper No. 380
publicationDetails.journalName: Cardozo Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Why set up evidentiary rules rather than allow factfinders to make decisions by considering all relevant evidence? This fundamental question has been the subject of unresolved controversy among scholars and policymakers since it was raised by Bentham at the beginning of the nineteenth century. This Essay offers a surprisingly straightforward answer: An economically minded legal system that processes many cases must suppress all evidence that brings along a negative productivity-expense balance. Failure to suppress inefficient evidence will result in serious diseconomies of scale. To operationalize this idea, I introduce a “signal-to-noise” method borrowed from statistics, science and engineering. This method focuses on the range of probabilities to which evidence falling into a specified category gives rise. Specifically, it compares the average probability associated with the given evidence (the “signal”) with the margins on both sides (the “noise”). This comparison allows policymakers to determine the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of evidence. When the evidence’s signal overpowers the noise, the legal system should admit the evidence. Conversely, when the noise emanating from the evidence drowns the signal, the evidence is inefficient and should therefore be excluded. I call this set of rules “the SNR principle.” Descriptively, I demonstrate that this principle best explains the rules of admissibility and corroboration by which our system selects evidence for trials. Prescriptively, I argue that the SNR principle should guide the rules of evidence-selection and determine the scope of criminal defendants’ constitutional right to compulsory process.

title: Mafia influence on voter participation in post-unification Italy
affiliations: University of Turin and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mafia influence on voter participation in post-unification Italy
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the Sicilian Mafia had already begun to influence electoral processes in the early decades of the Italian state. While the relationship between organized crime and politics in post-war Italy has been widely studied, little empirical evidence exists for the nineteenth century. The analysis exploits the large revision of electoral registers preceding the 1895 parliamentary election following the suffrage expansion introduced by the 1882 reform. Using municipal-level data for Sicily, the paper relates electoral absenteeism in 1895 to the change in the size of the electoral register between 1865 and 1895. To address the potential endogeneity of register changes, the expansion of the electorate is instrumented using a measure of pre-reform under-enfranchisement constructed from census information. The results show that the expansion of the electorate did not produce uniform effects across municipalities. While register growth is not associated with significant changes in absenteeism in municipalities without Mafia presence, a different pattern emerges in municipalities classified as Mafia areas. A finite mixture specification confirms the presence of heterogeneous participation regimes. These findings suggest that the functioning of electoral institutions in late nineteenth-century Sicily was shaped by local political environments and that Mafia influence may have affected electoral participation earlier than commonly assumed.

title: When Norms Don't Match: Normative Mismatch and the Biological Logic of Cooperation in International Politics

detail.title: When Norms Don't Match: Normative Mismatch and the Biological Logic of Cooperation in International Politics

detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of normative mismatch-the structural condition in which the factual cooperation structure of a group has expanded beyond the boundaries of its normative community-and derives from it a set of concrete, falsifiable predictions about current developments in international politics. The concept is grounded in the Biological Theory of Law (BTL), which holds that legal and moral norms are cooperation technology: instruments that evolved to solve the coordination problems of biological organisms with partly conflicting interests. When circumstances change faster than norms, the resulting mismatch produces predictable dysfunctions. This article applies the principle to four primary cases-US trade policy, military action against Iran, climate negotiations, and European dis/integration-and one deviant case-Chinese industrial policy-to demonstrate both the explanatory power and the boundary conditions of the theory. Each prediction is accompanied by explicit falsification criteria, including short-horizon indicators. A structured comparison with realism, liberalism, and constructivism demonstrates where the BTL generates predictions that these theories, individually or in combination, do not. The aim is not to replace existing theories but to demonstrate what a biologically grounded approach adds to their explanatory toolkit: a generative mechanism that predicts the direction of normative development, identifies when norms are structurally miscalibrated, and explains why interdependence sometimes produces cooperation and sometimes nationalism.

title: A Bootstrap Random Forest Approach to Predicting Business Innovation
affiliations: , Missouri University of Science and Technology and Missouri University of Science and Technology

detail.title: A Bootstrap Random Forest Approach to Predicting Business Innovation
detail.abstract: Despite a vast literature on business innovations, there remains limited global evidence on how internal capabilities, external exposure, and institutional conditions jointly predict innovation across diverse contexts. This study addresses that gap by providing a comprehensive assessment of innovation predictors using machine learning approaches. Drawing on World Bank Enterprise Survey data covering more than 100,000 firms in 122 countries, we apply a Bootstrap Forest model with test-set validation to examine predictors of product and process innovation. The results show that capital investment and formal worker training consistently emerge as the strongest predictors, accounting for at least one-fourth of the out-of-sample predictive power. At the same time, several widely discussed innovation barriers, such as ownership composition, gender of top management, and perceived institutional obstacles, display negligible predictive power. These results suggest that innovation is more closely associated with intentional investments in skills and capital than with static firm attributes or generalized institutional conditions. Subsample analysis reveals meaningful heterogeneities of second-tier-innovation predictors across regions and sectors: export intensity predicts innovation in Europe and Central Asia, while foreign-licensed technology predicts product innovation in Latin America and the Caribbean, and process and product innovations in service sectors. These differences highlight the need for policy approaches that combine broad capability-building priorities with context-specific complementary measures.

detail.abstract: On April 28, 2025, the Iberian Peninsula experienced a complete electrical blackout affecting 47 million people across Spain and Portugal. Drawing from the ENTSO-E investigation, this paper examines the policy implications of this event for power system management during rapid decarbonization. The investigation identified an unprecedented cascade of generation disconnections triggered by overvoltage conditions, tracing the root cause to institutional rather than technical failures: regulatory barriers prevented the utilization of renewable capacity with certified voltage control capability, market design incentives misaligned operational decisions with real-time stability requirements, and governance fragmentation impeded coordinated crisis response. These findings offer lessons for policymakers navigating the tension between market efficiency and system security in renewable-dominated grids.

title: Consciousness in Biological Organisms and Artificial Intelligence: The CRPBCE Theory of Accepted Object-Bound Complexity Reduction

detail.title: Consciousness in Biological Organisms and Artificial Intelligence: The CRPBCE Theory of Accepted Object-Bound Complexity Reduction
detail.abstract: This paper advances a single central claim: within the present framework, a necessary architectural condition for consciousness is that an organism be able to reduce a high-dimensional field of sensory or informational complexity, decide that this reduction is good enough, assign the result to an internal object, accept that object as linked to the ontological object in the world, and compare it either with a newly encountered object or with one already stored in memory. On this view, consciousness does not consist in preserving the full physical complexity of a phenomenon, but in forming and accepting a reduced internal object that the organism treats as the thing itself for the purposes of experience, memory, prediction, valuation, and action. The paper formalizes this idea within the Complexity-Reduction Across Physical, Biological, Cognitive, and Evolutionary Systems (CRPBCE) framework by distinguishing the full space of distinguishable alternatives from the reduced space preserved after compression, and by defining a reduction ratio, Ω CR , that quantifies the degree of accepted informational compression. However, compression alone is not sufficient. The decisive step is acceptance: the organism must determine that further refinement is not required under current biological or behavioral conditions, bind the reduced representation to an internal object, and place that object into operative relation with memory, comparison, and action. The examples and comparative discussions in the paper serve to support this main thesis. Heat is used as the canonical case showing how enormous physical complexity is transformed into a stable conscious object. Learned percepts and inherited templates illustrate how accepted reduction may arise through development or evolution. Bumblebee studies are used as empirical support for parts of the acceptance cycle, especially binding, comparison, and cost-sensitive decision. Artificial intelligence, quantum measurement, and holographic information bounds are included only as structural comparisons or boundary clarifications, not as the primary claim of the paper. In particular, the theory does not require quantum effects in order to explain consciousness at the level targeted here. The paper's key contribution is therefore not the generic claim that organisms compress information, but the stronger claim that, within the present framework, consciousness requires a system to treat a reduction as good enough, bind it to an object, accept that object as linked to the world, and compare it with memory. Consciousness, on this account, is accepted representational reduction. Crucially, this framework grounds consciousness in a quantity-the number of distinguishable alternatives (Boltzmann's W)-that already appears as a primitive in statistical mechanics and quantum theory. This sets it apart from existing frameworks, which either employ cognitive or information-theoretic primitives that are analogous to but not identical with W , or invoke thermodynamic quantities as structural analogies rather than as the primitive from which object-formation is derived. A principal implication of the framework is constructive: 1 CRPBCE specifies the minimal architectural conditions that any artificial system must satisfy in order to sustain perceived consciousness-the integrated, valenced, world-model-level perspective that a sufficiently general system has on its own accepted representations. This makes CRPBCE not only a theory of what consciousness is, but a blueprint for what an artificial system must implement to achieve it.

title: Adhering Indigenous Communities to the State: Recognition Politics During Civil Conflict
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Adhering Indigenous Communities to the State: Recognition Politics During Civil Conflict
detail.abstract: Numerous countries in recent decades have formally recognized collective indigenous claims to territory and self-governance during civil conflict despite challenges to state authority and social order. How does collective indigenous recognition impact conflict violence within communities? This paper shows that indigenous recognition can shore up order and state reach. It does so in Peru, where the state recognized thousands of indigenous communities during an internal conflict from 1980-2000 that disproportionately impacted indigenous Peruvians. Using a staggered difference-indifference research design and an original spatial mapping of conflict violence to indigenous communities, I find that formal recognition reduced wartime violence. Further analysis of community characteristics as well as state and community counterinsurgency efforts indicates that as recognition fosters greater legibility and transfers disputes into state institutions, it invites state penetration and coordination with state actors that ultimately adheres communities to the state.

title: A Bibliometric Analysis of the Most Frequently Used Theories in Global Research Publications (2015-2025)

detail.title: A Bibliometric Analysis of the Most Frequently Used Theories in Global Research Publications (2015-2025)
detail.abstract: This study examines the most frequently used theories in global research publications from 2015 to 2025 using a bibliometric approach. Grounded in Bibliometric Analysis and Scientometrics, the study analyzes peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science. A total of 1,200 articles were systematically selected and examined to identify recurring theoretical frameworks. Data were analyzed using frequency counts, ranking, and trend analysis. Results reveal that Constructivism, Social Learning Theory, Theory of Planned Behavior, and Systems Theory are among the most frequently utilized theories across disciplines. Findings also indicate a growing trend toward interdisciplinary and integrative theoretical approaches in recent years. The study contributes to the understanding of global research patterns and provides a reference for scholars in selecting appropriate theoretical frameworks.

title: A Deployed Cohort-Aware Counterfactual Imputation Pipeline for Measuring Staggered Rollouts Under Extreme Seasonality: Evidence from Affirm's BNPL Platform
affiliations: University of Waterloo and San Francisco

detail.title: A Deployed Cohort-Aware Counterfactual Imputation Pipeline for Measuring Staggered Rollouts Under Extreme Seasonality: Evidence from Affirm's BNPL Platform
detail.abstract: Evaluating product and policy changes in large-scale fintech platforms is an operational challenge: deployments are often staggered across partners for engineering and risk-management reasons, while strong seasonality makes simple pre/post comparisons unreliable and full A/B testing can be infeasible. This paper describes a deployed causal evaluation pipeline that measures the post-launch impact of a merchant-level product feature activated in staggered cohorts in a buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) platform using internal event logs. The pipeline constructs a merchant-week panel from high-volume transaction logs, assigns merchants to activation cohorts, and estimates average treatment effects on the treated (ATT) under staggered adoption by imputing counterfactual untreated outcomes for treated merchant-weeks. Counterfactuals are learned using only untreated observations and then imputed for treated periods in the potential-outcomes framework [15, 16]. In this application, cross-validation selects zero latent factors (𝑟 = 0), so the primary estimator reduces to a two-way fixed-effects counterfactual estimator (FEct) implemented as a special case of interactive fixed effects [5, 14]. As a robustness guardrail against cohort composition drift, the counterfactual surface is re-estimated with nuclear-norm matrix completion augmented with time-varying covariates that capture changes in purchasing behavior and risk composition [4]. Post-launch, the intervention increases confirmation rates by +2.99 percentage points (merchant-cluster bootstrap 𝑝 = 0.0018), with no statistically detectable change in approval rates. End-toend conversion increases by +1.68 percentage points but is not statistically distinguishable from zero over the observation window. Equivalence tests, placebo timing checks, and common-time falsification support the credibility of the estimate. While empirical magnitudes are specific to the BNPL setting, the cohort-aware imputation pipeline generalizes to any digital platform facing staggered rollouts and strong latent seasonality. detail.abstract: Many policy decisions involve trade-offs between lives and livelihoods. We provide the first estimates for a new welfare parameter that expresses this trade-off in the longevity-poverty space. To do so, we conduct randomized survey experiments with 20,000 respondents across seven middle-and high-income countries. Both the median and mean responses imply that individuals are willing to spend no more than about two years in poverty to gain one additional year of life, sharply restricting the plausible range for this normative parameter. We show how these estimates can inform policy trade-offs related to long-run global development, pandemic responses, and climate change.

detail.title: Colonial Genealogies of Marks and the Making of India’s Craft Identities: The Start of a Dialogue

publicationDetails.detailsText: Colonial Continuities, Global Shifts, and Digital Transformations in IPR

detail.abstract:
This chapter looks at collective and certification trademarks through the lens of India’s craft economy, asking what happens when a legal system built around individual ownership and formal markets is applied to deeply collective, informal ways of producing the final product of value. While trademarks are often imagined in terms of logos and brands, craft production presents a very different picture. The following chapter attempts to trace how this mismatch emerged historically, beginning with colonial trademark law, which prioritised imperial trade and merchant goodwill while leaving collective craft production legally undervalued. It then turns to the post-independence period, where crafts were governed largely through state-led institutions, certification schemes, and development policy, with trademark law arriving late and unevenly as a tool for collective identity.

Drawing on examples from textiles, pottery, and metal crafts, the chapter argues that collective and certification marks today operate more as socio-legal infrastructures. They organise membership, define authenticity, distribute authority, and shape who becomes visible in markets. While these marks can offer real benefits ranging from visibility to increased bargaining power, they can also reproduce internal hierarchies and discipline craft practices in subtle ways. The chapter ultimately argues that the key issue is not the existence of collective marks themselves, but the way they are governed, and whether trademark law has the space to genuinely treat collective labour and community authority as foundational principles.

title: Returning the Land: Toward a Species-First Framework for Nature-Based Solutions Design

detail.title: Returning the Land: Toward a Species-First Framework for Nature-Based Solutions Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and analytical paper. It does not involve human subjects, animal experimentation, or primary data collection requiring institutional ethical review. No ethics approval was required.

detail.abstract:
The decline of pollinators is commonly framed as a biodiversity crisis. This paper argues that it is more fundamentally a crisis of dispossession. Human land conversion has not merely degraded ecosystems; it has systematically displaced non-human species from the habitats in which they evolved. Yet contemporary Nature-based Solutions (NbS) continue to treat these species as if they can be reintroduced into landscapes defined by human objectives.

This paper identifies a structural flaw in prevailing NbS design: a human-first sequence, in which climate targets, funding constraints, and land availability are determined prior to ecological viability. Species are subsequently expected to occupy these predefined spaces, despite the absence of suitable habitat conditions.

In response, this study proposes the Species-First Framework (SFF), which reverses the design sequence. Rather than asking where humans wish to restore nature, the framework begins by identifying where displaced species can viably exist. It argues that effective ecological recovery depends not on the artificial placement of species, but on the return of habitat within landscapes that humans have neglected or abandoned for productive use.

The framework is operationalized through Elōra-X™, a wildflower-based restoration system applied to degraded coastal marine terraces in western Madagascar. These geomorphologically marginal terrains, largely unsuitable for agriculture or settlement expansion, are reinterpreted as viable habitats for native wildflowers and pollinator communities. By embedding livelihood generation within ecological function through apiculture, seed-based value chains, and community stewardship, the system reduces reliance on external incentives and supports long-term persistence. Its causal structure is formalized using ToC:f(x)™, enabling function-based verification of ecological and socio-economic outcomes.

This paper argues that Nature-based Solutions should not begin with the question of where humans intend to intervene, but with where non-human life can still belong. In this sense, restoration is not the construction of ecosystems, but the structured return of habitat to the species from which it was taken.

title: Structural Determinism in Climate Project Architecture: A Set-Theoretic and Invertibility-Based Foundation

detail.title: Structural Determinism in Climate Project Architecture: A Set-Theoretic and Invertibility-Based Foundation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects. Ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
The accelerating climate crisis exposes a fundamental limitation in contemporary climate project evaluation: most frameworks rely on probabilistic causality (P→Q), assuming that interventions may lead to desired outcomes. Under finite temporal and financial constraints, such probabilistic architectures are insufficient to ensure physically verifiable climate results.

This paper introduces a structural determinism framework grounded in set theory and inverse functional logic. A valid climate project is defined not by narrative alignment or expected correlation, but by structural inclusion: the intervention set P must be fully contained within the domain of legitimate physical climate outcomes Q, formally expressed as P ⊆ Q (equivalently, P − Q = ∅). Here, Q is defined as the intersection of climate-induced physical hazards (C) and directly affected human survival systems (H), i.e., Q = C ∩ H.

Within this formulation, project integrity is evaluated through structural purity, defined as |P ∩ Q| / |P|, which quantifies the proportion of project actions causally aligned with physical climate mitigation or adaptation. The framework further establishes invertibility (existence of f⁻¹) as a necessary condition for causal attribution and accountability, and formalizes structural drift as an entropic degradation of alignment over time.

By reframing climate impact as a set-theoretic and functional property rather than a probabilistic projection, this study advances a deterministic architecture for distinguishing structurally valid climate interventions from domain violations. The resulting framework provides a mathematical foundation for evaluating climate project legitimacy under finite time and capital constraints.

title: From Product to Practice: Geographical Indications and Productive Capacities in Traditional Textiles
affiliations: Queens University Belfast

detail.title: From Product to Practice: Geographical Indications and Productive Capacities in Traditional Textiles
detail.abstract: Geographical Indications (GIs) are often presented as the "best fit" IP tool for traditional textiles because they protect collective reputation and link products to place. Yet, in many textile contexts, GI protection delivers recognition without securing the conditions that make production possible. Names and reputations are protected, but the labour, skills, and social systems that sustain weaving, dyeing, printing, and other techniques remain economically and institutionally fragile. This paper argues that this gap is best understood by shifting the evaluative lens from products to productive capacities. Drawing on Cwik's productive capacities view, it treats cultural ownership as the ability of producer communities to sustain skilled labour, transmit knowledge across generations, organise collectively, and engage markets on fair, non-extractive terms. The article shows how product-centred specifications, authorised-user systems, and compliance-oriented control bodies can generate "visibility without empowerment," including through value capture by intermediaries. It then develops a practical agenda for reorienting GI governance using existing tools to move from fragile recognition to durable, people-centred ownership that supports living textile traditions over time.

title: Generative AI, Online Self-Presentation, and Labor Market Signaling: Evidence from LinkedIn Posting Behavior
affiliations: and Other Firms

detail.title: Generative AI, Online Self-Presentation, and Labor Market Signaling: Evidence from LinkedIn Posting Behavior
detail.abstract: We examine how the emergence of generative AI tools is associated with changes in LinkedIn employee posting behavior between 2019 and 2025. Using a novel dataset of daily LinkedIn posts by individual users worldwide, we document sharp increases in posting activity following major generative AI releases-notably OpenAI's public release of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022-and sustained growth through subsequent releases (GPT-4 in early 2023, Google's Gemini in late 2023, OpenAI's GPT-4o in mid-2024, and OpenAI o1 in late 2024). Descriptive evidence indicates an order-of-magnitude increase in average posts per employee over the sample period. To assess how communication content evolves, we analyze posts from a random sample of employees at two large technology firms, Apple and Microsoft, using natural language processing methods. We find that while basic length measures (words, tokens, and sentences) follow gradual upward trends that predate the AI shock, features related to structure, formatting, and style exhibit sharper post-2022 shifts. In particular, posts become more segmented, organized, and expressive, with substantial increases in paragraph breaks, bullet-point usage, and emoji use; lexical diversity increases more modestly and mainly during later diffusion waves. Regression estimates show that these post-2022 patterns persist after controlling for individual characteristics, job roles, departments, seniority, company affiliation, and time effects. Overall, the results suggest that generative AI has reduced the cost of professional self-presentation and altered the form and style of online labor market signaling. While these changes may broaden visibility and communication confidence, they also raise concerns about the informational content of professional signals. We conclude with implications for labor market signaling and directions for future research on the causal and distributional effects of AI-assisted communication.

title: Altruism, Mutually Assured Temptation, and Preferences over Prisoner's Dilemmas
affiliations: Economics Department, University of Bath and Loyola University Maryland

detail.title: Altruism, Mutually Assured Temptation, and Preferences over Prisoner's Dilemmas
detail.abstract: Material payoffs tempt altruistic decision makers in isolation to sacrifice their virtuous commitments towards the society. Accordingly, they wish to ex-ante avoid more tempting decision-making environments in a two-stage framework where they first choose an environment and then an action within it. However, the notions of virtue and vice at the group level are philosophically problematic to define or predict. To address these issues, we extend the analysis to strategic settings where instead of decision-making environments, altruistic individuals first choose between prisoner's dilemma games with more or less tempting material payoffs and then play the game. Our focus on Prisoner's dilemma games is because these are classic models of social situations where both altruism and temptation co-exist naturally. We find that, in contrast to isolated decision makers who always fall for temptation and hence may avoid more tempting environments if given a choice, games with higher temptation can enhance cooperation among altruistic players. This curious possibility in the second stage implies that, in the first stage, a group of non-cooperative players may prefer prisoner's dilemma games with higher temptation as they agree, counterintuitively, that greed can enhance cooperation towards achieving their altruistic goals. We then show that material and psychological payoffs are aligned in equilibrium, so both materialist planners and decentralized altruistic agents may rationally select, ex-ante, more tempting games to better achieve both materialistic and altruistic ends.

title: The Ontological Relationship Between the Knowledge Economy and the Techno-Feudal Order: A Story of Usurpation, Not Continuity

detail.title: The Ontological Relationship Between the Knowledge Economy and the Techno-Feudal Order: A Story of Usurpation, Not Continuity
detail.abstract: This paper explores the ontological disconnect between the traditional "Knowledge Economy" and the emerging "Techno-feudal" order. It argues that the transition between these two regimes does not constitute a linear evolution or digital progress, but rather a structural usurpation. While the knowledge economy posits the human being as an epistemic subject and the generator of value through intellect, the techno-feudal order reduces the human to a passive source of behavioral data. The paper identifies the "knowledge economy" discourse as a contemporary veil of legitimacy-a dual-layered ontological fraud-that masks the systemic liquidation of human agency. Furthermore, it critiques the role of progressive and humanist actors who, by focusing on superficial ethical regulations, inadvertently provide consent to this epistemic displacement.

title: The Role of Finance in Supporting the Transition Toward the Circular Economy
affiliations: GREEN Research Centre - Bocconi University

detail.title: The Role of Finance in Supporting the Transition Toward the Circular Economy
detail.abstract: This paper aims to explore a new field of research on the relations between finance and the Circular Economy (CE). As a powerful driver of change in the real economy, the CE represents both a source of opportunities and a generator of threats for financial institutions that directly invest in non-financial companies, such as banks and specialized investors (for ex. private equity and private debt funds). First of all, literature on companies financing and, on the role, played by the financial system in supporting the growth of the real economy is explored, also considering specific features such as the finance for innovation and R&D. The goal is to point out the main elements that affect the company-financer relationship and the way the CE paradigm can positively influence and change them. Furthermore, an analysis on the changing shape of the economic activity provoked by the transition toward the CE, in terms of both business economics profile and sources of volatility, is carried out in order to understand what the opportunities and the threats are generated on the side of financial actors. Finally, the impact that the circular business models generate on the main credit risk metrics is considered, in order to understand what the major changes are financial institutions have to introduce in order to catch the advantages generated in terms of better creditworthiness of their counterparts. The CE offers some interesting opportunities to financial players, in terms of both more stable economics and a lower risk profile in the long period, but, at the same time, it asks for introducing important changes in the chain of activities of financial players. Only if financial actors deploy those changes inside their organizations, as well as improving their risk appetite in the short term, they will be able to catch the corresponding advantages, in terms of both investment opportunities and their superior sustainability in the long run.

title: Circumstances, Culture, and Inequality of Opportunity in Mexico: Integrating Roemer's Framework with Lamont's Cultural Processes Theory

detail.title: Circumstances, Culture, and Inequality of Opportunity in Mexico: Integrating Roemer's Framework with Lamont's Cultural Processes Theory
detail.abstract: This paper integrates Roemer’s ex-ante inequality of opportunity (IOp) frame­work with Lamont et al. (2014) cultural processes theory (racialization, stigma­tization, standardization, and evaluation) to both measure and interpret IOp in Mexico. Using nationally representative data from the ESRU-EMOVI 2023 sur­vey (N = 13,164), we apply conditional inference trees with Shapley value decomposition across a standard (K = 9) and an expanded (K = 12) spec­ification. IOp accounts for 26.6% to 30.6% of total income inequality (MLD). Household economic conditions at origin emerge as the single most impor­tant circumstance (20.8%), displacing parental education and occupation. Sex is the second-largest contributor (14.6%) and remains stable when household wealth is controlled, revealing gender-based evaluation as an independent IOp source. Geographic circumstances explain over a quarter of IOp through ter­ritorial stigmatization. Skin tone contributes modestly (1.1–2.4%), suggesting racialization operates as a distal process mediated through household wealth and educational access. Cohort analysis reveals declining total inequality (p < 0.001) alongside a suggestive increase in the IOp share (p = 0.061). These findings demonstrate that integrating cultural theory with quantitative measurement enriches both the estimation and interpretation of how birth circumstances shape economic outcomes.

title: Exchange Rate Expectations and Currency Demand
affiliations: University of Geneva

detail.title: Exchange Rate Expectations and Currency Demand
detail.abstract: This paper develops a new method to extract exchange rate expectations from investment positions. I use relative allocations between otherwise identical exchange-traded funds (ETFs) offered with and without a currency hedge to measure investors' pure currency demand and infer a distribution of currency return expectations. These portfolioimplied expectations predict future exchange rates more accurately than survey-based expectations or expectations derived from macroeconomic models or currency pricing factors. Dispersion in portfolio-implied expectations accounts for 27% of exchange rate volatility, consistent with models of heterogeneous beliefs.

title: Hardware-Efficient 3D Medical Segmentation: Bridging the Dimensionality Gap in Vision Foundation Models via Spatial Continuity Regularization
affiliations: SRM Institute of Science and Technology and SRM Institute of Science and Technology

detail.title: Hardware-Efficient 3D Medical Segmentation: Bridging the Dimensionality Gap in Vision Foundation Models via Spatial Continuity Regularization
detail.abstract: Vision foundation models, such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM-3), have demonstrated exceptional zero-shot generalization in 2D medical image segmentation but often fail to maintain spatial coherence in 3D volumetric data. This dimensionality gap results in "staircase" artifacts and anatomically implausible reconstructions, undermining clinical utility. In this work, we investigate the trade-offs between computational efficiency and 3D consistency when adapting 2D foundation models to volumetric MRI and CT datasets. We first report a negative result: a Cross-Plane Contrastive Learning (CPCL) framework designed to enforce orthogonal consistency across axial, coronal, and sagittal views. While theoretically sound, CPCL introduces a prohibitive computational bottleneck, requiring over 40 GB of VRAM and a 4.5-fold increase in training latency, rendering iterative fine-tuning unfeasible in resource-constrained environments. To address these limitations, we propose Spatial Continuity Regularization (SCR-SAM), a lightweight longitudinal "tethering" strategy that optimizes adjacent slice pairs. Experimental results on BraTS (MRI) and KiTS (CT) datasets demonstrate that SCR-SAM reduces the Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) by approximately 79% on MRI volumes while maintaining a stable peak training VRAM of only 12.70 GB on standard Tesla T4 hardware. By preserving the semantic power of the 2D vision encoder without the overhead of complex 3D architectures, SCR-SAM provides a robust, hardware-accessible pathway for high-fidelity volumetric medical segmentation.

title: Who Owns Crypto in the Euro Area? Drivers of Crypto Adoption, Payment Use, and its Interaction with Fiat Cash
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Who Owns Crypto in the Euro Area? Drivers of Crypto Adoption, Payment Use, and its Interaction with Fiat Cash
detail.abstract: Using a survey of 39,507 adults in 17 euro-area countries, I find that crypto-asset owners and the niche subgroup of payers have distinct profiles. Owners – typically younger, male, and financially active – exhibit mixed preferences, valuing both cash-like privacy and card-like speed. Crypto payers display a cash-centric profile, seeking to replicate physical cash’s privacy and ease of use in digital form. While standard specifications show that holding cash reserves is positively associated with owning crypto – challenging the view that early adopters reject cash –, a multiple-instrument IV strategy exploiting pandemic-related payment shocks reveals a causal sign reversal: for compliers, building precautionary cash buffers reduces the probability of crypto ownership under uncertainty. These findings (1) explain the ownership-payment wedge as driven by user profiles beyond merchant-acceptance frictions, (2) show crypto and cash act as portfolio complements but substitutes under stress, and (3) may inform crypto regulation and CBDC design.

title: How Cyclone Traps People into Poverty: Empirical Evidence from Bangladesh
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: How Cyclone Traps People into Poverty: Empirical Evidence from Bangladesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used previously collected survey data. All participants provided informed consent at the time of the survey, and the research was conducted in accordance with relevant ethical guidelines. No new data collection involving human subjects was performed.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether a poverty trap emerges in the aftermath of a disaster, what determines its depth in terms of income level, and whether consumption-side factors contribute to its persistence. It focuses on the coastal region of Bangladesh affected by Cyclone Aila in May 2009 and empirically analyzes how disaster coping strategies influence asset growth. The impact of Aila on the extent of poverty traps is assessed by comparing affected areas with a control group of unaffected regions, using primary data from approximately 890 households in coastal Bangladesh. The theoretical framework demonstrates that when production is non-convex, disaster-induced asset losses can generate poverty traps, pushing households toward a lower equilibrium among multiple equilibria at different asset levels. Employing both semi-parametric and parametric approaches, the findings reveal multiple equilibria in asset index–based trajectories in disaster-affected areas, indicating the presence of a poverty trap, whereas income convergence between high- and low-income households is observed in unaffected areas. The results further suggest that the depth of the poverty trap is reduced for households able to shift to a higher-income equilibrium, and, based on a natural experimental design, poorer households in affected areas are more likely to remain trapped at lower income levels compared to those in unaffected regions.

title: Agentic AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and the Institutional Turn: Legal Architectures and Financial Governance in the Age of Distributional AGI

detail.title: Agentic AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and the Institutional Turn: Legal Architectures and Financial Governance in the Age of Distributional AGI
detail.abstract: The proliferation of agentic artificial intelligence systems-characterized by autonomous goal-seeking, tool use, and multi-agent coordination-presents unprecedented challenges to existing legal and financial regulatory frameworks. While traditional AI governance has focused on model-level alignment through training-time interventions such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), the deployment of large language models (LLMs) as persistent agents embedded within socio-technical systems necessitates a paradigm shift toward institutional governance structures. This paper examines the intersection of agentic AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and their implications for legal accountability and financial market integrity. Through a comprehensive analysis of the Institutional AI framework proposed by Pierucci et al. [1], we argue that alignment must be reconceptualized as a mechanism design problem involving runtime governance graphs, sanction functions, and observable behavioral constraints rather than internalized constitutional values. We address the critical deficit identified by LeCun regarding the absence of world models in current agents, demonstrating how RAG architectures function as externalized epistemic infrastructure that grounds agentic cognition in verifiable data repositories. The paper subsequently interrogates the legal implications of these systems under the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) and the regulatory thresholds established by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and European Central Bank (ECB), proposing justified compliance boundaries for high-risk financial applications. Furthermore, we acknowledge significant governance gaps within Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols where institutional oversight mechanisms face structural limitations. By synthesizing technical insights from multi-agent systems, constitutional AI limitations, and offensive security frameworks, this work advances a jurisprudential foundation for agentic AI that prioritizes defensible audit trails, incentive-compatible compliance, and systemic stability over opaque internal alignment guarantees. The analysis concludes that the future of AI governance lies not in perfecting isolated model behavior, but in architecting institutional environments where compliant behavior emerges as the dominant strategy through carefully calibrated payoff landscapes.
