title: Monetary Policy under Multiple Financing Constraints
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Research Department and European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research

detail.title: Monetary Policy under Multiple Financing Constraints
detail.abstract: We revisit the credit channel of monetary policy when firms face multiple financing constraints, a common feature of corporate financing we document empirically. Our theory shows that the multiplicity of constraints dampens the transmission of expansionary policy to firm borrowing and investment notably but amplifies the transmission of policy tightening. This asymmetry arises because, when policy tightens (eases), the most (least) responsive constraint binds. Using U.S. firm-level data and exploiting a quasi-natural experiment, we find strong support for these predictions and for our proposed channel. Embedding the mechanism into a New Keynesian framework, we find that the drop in investment after contractionary shocks is twice as large as its increase following equally-sized expansionary shocks, thus providing an explanation for why monetary policy tightenings have stronger effects than easings, a longstanding puzzle in monetary economics. Moreover, our analysis implies that the effectiveness of monetary policy is strongly determined by the distribution of financial constraints across firms and that similar asymmetries likely characterize the transmission of other macroeconomic shocks.

title: Dynamic Credit Constraints: Theory and Evidence from Credit Lines
affiliations: Sveriges Riksbank, Sveriges Riksbank - Research Division, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business - Finance and Business Economics Department and Sveriges Riksbank - Research Division

detail.title: Dynamic Credit Constraints: Theory and Evidence from Credit Lines
detail.abstract: We use a comprehensive Swedish credit register to document that firms across the size distribution have access to substantial borrowing capacity via credit lines. However, most firms choose not to use all available credit, even though interest rates are low compared to their return on equity. The low utilization of credit is consistent with a theoretical model in which utilization rates decrease with both real and financial uncertainty. We estimate the model structurally at the firm level and find that financial uncertainty driven by liquidity shocks is much more important than real uncertainty driven by cash flow shocks for explaining the low utilization of credit.

title: When Environmental Policy Backfires: Air Pollution Warnings and Influenza Transmission in South Korea
affiliations: Auburn University

detail.title: When Environmental Policy Backfires: Air Pollution Warnings and Influenza Transmission in South Korea
detail.abstract: Air-quality warnings aim to protect public health by reducing outdoor exposure but may generate unintended behavioral spillovers. Using daily province-level data from South Korea (2015–2019) and exploiting the staggered rollout of real-time Emergency Disaster Texts (EDT), I show that particulate matter (PM) warnings increase influenza incidence through an information-driven behavioral response. A difference-in-differences analysis finds that post-warning flu incidence rises significantly after EDT implementation, an effect absent in the pre-EDT period. Event-study estimates reveal no pre-trend, with incidence beginning to rise around day 3 and peaking 25–40 days after an alert — consistent with secondary transmission chains seeded by warning-induced indoor congregation rather than a single incubation cycle. Online search data confirm that warnings trigger rapid substitution toward commercial indoor venues, with behavioral reversion within two days, supporting the interpretation that a brief congregation episode generates a prolonged epidemiological arc. Effects are concentrated among school-aged children and stronger in areas with greater alert exposure. Falsification tests show that physical pollution shocks predict external-organ conditions such as dermatitis, while only the warning signal predicts influenza, isolating an informational behavioral channel from direct biological exposure. These findings highlight nontrivial hidden externalities in environmental alert design and suggest that coupling pollution warnings with indoor hygiene guidance could mitigate the unintended epidemiological costs of high-salience alert systems.

title: Resource Tenure Issues in the Settlement of Sudan's Dislocated Population

detail.title: Resource Tenure Issues in the Settlement of Sudan's Dislocated Population
detail.abstract: The number of displaced people in Sudan as a result of conflict and famine over nearly two decades of war has been estimated to be in the millions. The lengthy period of time that many local populations have been dislocated and the consequent disruption of food producing activities poses complicated problems in both near-term food security and the longer-term rehabilitation of the country's traditional agricultural sector. Recovery of households and production systems after years of conflict and famine for the displaced will involve more than simply a return to home areas. Resource use and access arrangements, will emerge contested and reconfigured as claimants with perceived rights based on various past customary and state tenure regimes seek to exercise these rights in a changed human and biophysical landscape. This paper will examine some of the land tenure issues likely to become important as large populations of Sudan's internally displaced seek to re-engage in agricultural production systems they are familiar with. In the more populous agriculturally endowed locations where the recovery of many households and numerous production systems will initially be focused, establishing or re-establishing a mutually agreed upon tenure system (or set of systems) and modes of resource use and access that are widely seen as equitable, secure, inclusive and legitimate at the national level will, while complicated, be important to agricultural production, and food security.

title: Multidimensional Screening with Element-wise Monotone Independence
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Students

detail.title: Multidimensional Screening with Element-wise Monotone Independence
detail.abstract: This paper develops a Myersonian approach to multidimensional screening with a finite action set. The principal's objective admits a virtual-surplus representation that yields score-based allocation rules. We identify a simple multidimensional regularity condition-element-wise monotone independence-under which the score-maximizing allocation rule is globally optimal and implementable. The result delivers a tractable characterization of optimal multidimensional mechanisms through virtual values and deterministic scoring rules.

title: Can the Trump Administration’s Decision not to Participate in BEPS 2.0 be Justified in Terms of Political Right?
affiliations: National Law University Delhi

detail.title: Can the Trump Administration’s Decision not to Participate in BEPS 2.0 be Justified in Terms of Political Right?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is my assignment submitted as a part of internal assessment at the Warwick, University.

detail.abstract:
On the 20th of January, alongside numerous controversial executive orders, United States of America (US) President Donald Trump issued a surprising executive order affirming that the US would opt out of the OECD initiative BEPS 2.0. Further, the US Treasury Secretary must develop options for a response to be presented to the President in 60 days, specifically by March 21, 2025. On the 3rd of February, the US also opted out of the United Nations (UN) Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation. Following the US decision to pull out of the Global Tax Deal, countries such as India, for instance, are sceptical after signing global tax agreements without the support of one of the world’s most powerful nations’ economies.

Political rhetoric aside, this essay answers a different yet significant theoretical question often forgotten when assessing Trump’s move: Can the Trump administration’s decision not to participate in BEPS 2.0 be justified in terms of “political right”?

Political right, in relation to international business taxation, is understood as the legal ramifications of political and diplomatic decisions made in tax policy. The decisions are made through tax statutes or bilateral and multilateral taxing treaties. Tax politics can be understood as a national government’s response to manage the geopolitical tension behind taxes, both politically and diplomatically. The geopolitical aspect of taxation is the scarce resource of investment capital, for instance, foreign direct investment (FDI), and tax co-operation or competition (as an aspect of tax policy). While these are operational ways in which tax politics have been pursued to manage that scarcity, ensuring this means that tax policy choices, including corporate income tax rate choices, made in the national interest may not necessarily be within the global welfare norms. The interests of multinational groups (MNGs) and the national interest of national governing bodies do not always align. It is this misalignment that could have a dubious effect on the formation of taxation policy, and therefore on the political right of taxation policy.

This paper argues that Trump’s decision to leave BEPS 2.0 was justifiable when viewed from a complex and multifaceted “political right” perspective.  In the first place, the Republican Party is viewed as a far-right party. The exercise of political rights would mean favouring market freedom and limited government. The two-pillar solution can impose global tax standards that would likely restrict free market choices and favour government involvement in the economy, which conflicts with the Republican Party’s core values.  Second, based on game theory, it is argued that the decision to abstain from BEPS 2.0, specifically the elements that pertain to the allocation of taxing rights to market jurisdictions and a global minimum tax regime in source countries, can be characterised as a strategic and prudent choice. While controversial, the decision will help preserve the tax revenue from their large high-tech conglomerate.

title: Arts of Witness: Resilience Amid Technological Acceleration, Geopolitical Volatility, and Media Transformation in Contemporary South Asia

detail.title: Arts of Witness: Resilience Amid Technological Acceleration, Geopolitical Volatility, and Media Transformation in Contemporary South Asia

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self Funded

detail.abstract: This paper develops the concept of the 'Arts of Witness' as a framework for understanding resilience in an age defined by technological acceleration, geopolitical volatility, and media transformation. Drawing on ethnographic experience spanning the 2014 Wembley Stadium address by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and UK Prime Minister David Cameron, the digitised isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic, and first-hand reporting from the 2021 G20 Rome Summit, the study situates South Asia within a broader global reconfiguration of power and narrative authority. Engaging leadership theory, brand strategy, and media ethics scholarship alongside contemporary reports from the World Economic Forum, Reuters Institute, and European Commission, the paper argues that witnessing has shifted from a largely Western-exported normative practice into a multidirectional, contested, and technologically mediated performance. It examines the rise of Artificial Intelligence in journalism, regulatory pressures on media institutions, and the tension between traditional professional journalism and social media ecosystems. The paper concludes that the Arts of Witness represent not merely documentation but an ethical assertion of meaning and accountability. In an era where algorithms shape visibility and geopolitical narratives are fiercely contested, understanding how we witness-through which platforms, under what political pressures, and within which cultural frameworks-is central to navigating the future of democratic discourse.

title: From Protecting Competitors to Protecting Competition: The Past, Present, and Future of the Robinson-Patman Act
affiliations: Department of Justice and

detail.title: From Protecting Competitors to Protecting Competition: The Past, Present, and Future of the Robinson-Patman Act
detail.abstract: Nearly a century has passed since the enactment of the Robinson-Patman Act (RPA). An amendment to the Clayton Act, the RPA sits uncomfortably under the umbrella of American antitrust law. Among its many unique features is its proscription of price discrimination that harms competition. A fundamental question, therefore, is how a price discrimination law can operate to facilitate the goal of antitrust. This paper attempts to answer that question. This article argues that the history, structure, and text of the RPA require courts to evaluate the RPA’s competitive-effects language consistent with the other provisions of the Clayton Act and the broader antitrust laws. The RPA is principally concerned with two types of conduct: primary and secondary line. The Supreme Court has harmonized the former with the broader antitrust laws. Drawing on the history, structure, and text of the RPA, this article argues that courts should employ the raising rivals’ costs framework when evaluating secondary-line theories of harm.

title: The Unintended Consequences of Low Emission Zones: Evidence from Madrid Central
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin)

detail.title: The Unintended Consequences of Low Emission Zones: Evidence from Madrid Central
detail.abstract: We investigate the spillover effects of low emission zones on traffic, air pollution, and health, focusing on Madrid Central. Combining satellite and  station-level air quality data with nearly 4,000 traffic sensors, we find that while the policy reduced NO2 and PM2.5 inside the restricted area, it displaced  traffic by 2.7 percent city-wide, generating heterogeneous spillovers: PM2.5 increased by up-to 0.4 µg/m3 in some districts while decreasing in others. Two        spatial channels shape these spillovers: wind transport carries cleaner air from the restriction zone to downwind neighborhoods, while more distant districts  bear the full cost of rerouted traffic. These pollution increases fall disproportionately on lower-income peripheral neighborhoods. Comparing districts by the     direction of their estimated pollution change, we find suggestive evidence of higher hospitalization and mortality rates in pollution-increase vis-à-vis  pollution-decrease districts. These findings suggest that geographically targeted driving restrictions can redistribute pollution in ways that systematically  disadvantage peripheral communities.

title: Green Silence: Double Machine Learning Carbon Emissions Under Sample Selection Bias
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Adam Smith Business School, EDHEC Business School and Swiss Finance Institute - University of Geneva

detail.title: Green Silence: Double Machine Learning Carbon Emissions Under Sample Selection Bias
detail.abstract: Voluntary carbon disclosure creates a paradox where firms strategically choose whether to report emissions, with high emitters often remaining silent to exploit estimation biases. This selfselection problem distorts climate risk pricing and policy analysis. We propose a three-step Heckman-inspired framework for high-dimensional data using kernel group lasso, double machine learning, and peer firm information. An empirical study of 3,444 U.S. firms (2010-2023) finds strong evidence of selection bias. Naïve imputation methods underestimate emissions, leading to a $2.6 billion carbon tax shortfall and up to $525 billion in hidden social costs. Correcting for non-disclosure bias reveals a higher carbon premium.

title: Geographical Indications and Authorised Users in India: A Critical Analysis with Special Reference to Muga Silk of Assam

detail.title: Geographical Indications and Authorised Users in India: A Critical Analysis with Special Reference to Muga Silk of Assam
detail.abstract: The effectiveness of the Geographical Indications (GI) regime in India significantly depends on the participation of "Authorised Users" (AUs), who are legally empowered to use registered GIs. While India has witnessed substantial growth in GI registrations, the number of authorised users remains disproportionately low. This paper critically examines the concept, legal framework, and practical challenges relating to authorised users under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, with a focused case study on Muga Silk of Assam. It argues that the under-utilisation of AU registration undermines the objectives of GI protection and proposes reforms to enhance inclusivity, enforcement, and economic impact.

title: Ayn Rand and Kingfisher on Zero-Carbon Bombs and a Sustainable Future
affiliations: Phenikaa University

detail.title: Ayn Rand and Kingfisher on Zero-Carbon Bombs and a Sustainable Future
detail.abstract: This piece imagines a fictional dialogue between Rand and Kingfisher, a philosopher-bird, centering on Rand’s key assumptions in the context of climate change, biodiversity loss, and environmental crises.

title: Foreign Ownership and Environmental Performance Under the EU Emissions Trading System
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome, Sapienza University of Rome, Second University of Naples, Sapienza University of Rome and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Foreign Ownership and Environmental Performance Under the EU Emissions Trading System

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the European Union – Next Generation EU, Mission 4, Component 1, under PRIN 2022, CUP B53D23010080006.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the environmental consequences of foreign acquisitions in a highly regulated setting, focusing on plant-level outcomes in Italy under Phase III of the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS). Combining verified emissions data with ownership and financial information for 2013-2020, we identify causal effects using a staggered Difference-inDifferences approach with Generalized Propensity Score weighting. Our baseline results suggest that foreign acquisition has a statistically insignificant effect on total emissions, but leads to a substantial reduction in emission intensity, without significant changes in output. Importantly, we find that the environmental effects vary by the origin of the investor: acquisitions by firms from OECD or EU-ETS countries improve emission efficiency, whereas those from non-OECD or non-EU-ETS countries exhibit less favourable outcomes. These findings provide new evidence on the role of regulatory experience and technological capabilities in shaping the environmental impact of foreign investment, highlighting the importance of accounting for investor origin when assessing FDI's environmental consequences.

title: orGAN: Bridging Synthetic and Real Data for Surgical AI via Consistent Image–Label Generation
affiliations: University of Tokyo - The University of Tokyo, University of Tokyo and University of Tokyo

detail.title: orGAN: Bridging Synthetic and Real Data for Surgical AI via Consistent Image–Label Generation
detail.abstract: \textbf{Background and Objective:} Deep learning in medical imaging faces challenges including restricted data diversity, ethical constraints, high data acquisition costs, and limited accurate annotations. Accurately identifying and localizing bleeding sources during surgery is especially difficult due to scarce, well-annotated, realistic datasets. We propose orGAN, a framework for generating realistic, annotated synthetic surgical images of bleeding scenarios to mitigate these limitations. \textbf{Methods:} The orGAN pipeline uses an enhanced StyleGAN3 architecture tailored to silicone-based “mimicking organs” that emulate tissue properties. The system synthesizes bleeding images with specified bleeding coordinates and simultaneously extracts coordinates and masks to provide artifact-free supervision signals. An inpainting network refines images, and Bleeding Alert Map (BAM) models are trained on a balanced 1:1 dataset blending orGAN synthetic data with “mimicking organ” images. The software is implemented as a modular, reproducible pipeline with clear interfaces for downstream training. \textbf{Results:} The enhanced StyleGAN3 achieved an Inception Score increase of 2.24, and the inpainting network maintained a mean SSIM of 0.98. BAM trained on the blended dataset reached 90\% image-level bleeding detection accuracy and up to 99\% frame-level accuracy in both ex-vivo and in-vivo evaluations, outperforming models trained solely on real or solely on synthetic data. \textbf{Conclusions:} orGAN provides an ethical and economical approach to generating annotated surgical datasets, coupling high-fidelity image synthesis with automatic supervision (coordinates and masks). The modular design enables reuse beyond one-off experiments and supports bleeding-localization workflows and broader AI applications in surgery.

title: Acquisition Reporting Complexity and Post-acquisition Misreporting
affiliations: University of Louisville, University of Louisiana Monroe and University of Tennessee, Haslam College of Business, Accounting and Information Management

detail.title: Acquisition Reporting Complexity and Post-acquisition Misreporting
detail.abstract: Mergers and acquisitions (M&As) are significant corporate events offering many benefits to firms. However, because they are complex, they can lead to post-acquisition financial reporting problems. We focus on two components of acquisition reporting complexity – acquisition accounting complexity, which is related to the recording of the M&A transaction following Accounting Standards Codification 805 Business Combinations, and acquisition integration complexity, which results from the reporting of new transactions in the post-acquisition integration period. We find that acquisition reporting complexity increases the likelihood of post-acquisition misreporting but, importantly, this misreporting is driven by acquisition integration complexity rather than acquisition accounting complexity. We further find that acquisition reporting complexity, particularly acquisition integration complexity, increases the amount of time taken to discover post-acquisition misstatements as well as their magnitude.

title: Does the Presence of Multinationals Help Domestic Firms to Comply with Environmental Regulations? Evidence from Italy
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome, Sapienza University of Rome, Second University of Naples, Sapienza University of Rome and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Does the Presence of Multinationals Help Domestic Firms to Comply with Environmental Regulations? Evidence from Italy

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the European Union – Next Generation EU, Mission 4, Component 1, under PRIN 2022, CUP B53D23010080006.

detail.abstract: Countries worldwide implement various policy instruments to mitigate and prevent environmental degradation. Within the European Union, the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) is a central mechanism aimed at reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This paper investigates how the presence of foreign-owned firms influences the environmental performance of domestic firms subject to the ETS, particularly those operating in power and heat generation and energy-intensive sectors. Using plant-level data from Italy for the period 2013-2020-corresponding to the third phase of the EU ETS-we find that the presence of foreign-owned suppliers facilitates compliance by domestic plants, leading to a reduction in emission intensity (measured as emissions per unit of output). In contrast, the presence of foreign-owned customers and competitors appears to have an adverse effect, although the influence of the foreign competition is less statistically robust.

title: Collective Bargaining Centralisation Against All Odds? The Italian Telecommunications Industry after Market Liberalization

detail.title: Collective Bargaining Centralisation Against All Odds? The Italian Telecommunications Industry after Market Liberalization
detail.abstract: The widespread trends towards markets liberalisation, decline in trade union power, and flexible work organization were expected to push collective bargaining institutions to converge to a decentralised bargaining structure. This crude version of the neoliberal convergence thesis, however, was not borne out. Instead, change in employment relations has been more nuanced than initially thought. This paper explores the conditions under which centralisation of bargaining is possible, even in a more competitive environment with pressures for greater flexibility. It draws on case study evidence from the Italian telecommunications industry, tracing back the process of liberalisation since the early 1990s. It is shown how the strategies and the coalitions between organised labour, business and the state explain in large part this path of institutional change.

reference: Relations industrielles, volume 69, issue 2, 2014[10.7202/1025032ar]
title: Institutional Change in Greek Industrial Relations in an Era of Fiscal Crisis
affiliations: University of the West of England (UWE) - Bristol Business School and

detail.title: Institutional Change in Greek Industrial Relations in an Era of Fiscal Crisis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Relations industrielles, volume 69, issue 2, 2014[10.7202/1025032ar]

detail.abstract: The main aim of this paper is to contribute to the ongoing debate on the facets of the Greek crisis via an analysis of the changes in the institutional framework of the labour market that are introduced as a result of the EU/IMF mechanism for financial support. The paper tries to make sense of the immense transformations in the Greek industrial relations system and to evaluate the direction of change, using insights from the varieties of capitalism literature. In this strand of literature it is well established that the comparative institutional advantage and high economic performance of a country depends on its overall institutional arrangement and the fit between different institutions (including the industrial relations sphere). Thus, it is important to examine the current injection of liberal market elements in the Greek industrial relations realm vis-à-vis the wider institutional context. This will allow us to gauge the suitability and chances for the implementation of IMF’s ‘one-size-fits-all’ policies.

title: Glass Barriers in Income Distributions
affiliations: ADA University

detail.title: Glass Barriers in Income Distributions
detail.abstract: We introduce glass barriers: income levels at which the density reaches a local minimum, creating structural gaps that impede upward mobility. A glass barrier at percentile p * is simultaneously a local maximum of the Lorenz curvature L ′′ (p *), a local maximum of asymptotic quantile estimation variance, and a local minimum of the Fisher information for the income quantile-a new information-theoretic characterisation. We propose a nonparametric estimator with bootstrap inference and validate it in a Monte Carlo study: detection rates exceed 90% for moderate and sharp barriers at n ≥ 1,000 with bootstrap coverage approaching nominal at survey-scale sample sizes.

title: Labour Market Integration and Firm Wages: Evidence from the European Union
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Labour Market Integration and Firm Wages: Evidence from the European Union

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the European Union – Next Generation EU, Mission 4, Component 1, under PRIN 2022, CUP B53D23010080006.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how increased labour market integration across countries affects firm-level wages, focusing on the period following the European Union (EU) enlargement in 2004. Using firm-level wage data from EU countries over the period 2004-2012, combined with regionallevel migration data, we find that a higher presence of foreign workers within a region is associated with wage reductions in firms located in the old EU member states (the West), and with wage increases in firms based in the new EU member states (the East). Consequently, rising labour mobility within the enlarged EU contributes to wage convergence between these two groups of countries.

title: Clientelism, Institutions, and Sovereign Default
affiliations: SUNY Stony Brook - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Clientelism, Institutions, and Sovereign Default
detail.abstract: Emerging economies exhibit pro-cyclical fiscal policy, counter-cyclical sovereign spreads, and recurrent debt crises, whereas advanced economies sustain high debt with low spreads and lower volatility in outcomes. We document that these differences are systematically related to institutional strength, measured by horizontal accountability, and to the prevalence of clientelistic allocation of public resources in a panel of 51 countries (1994-2023). We develop a dynamic political-economy model of sovereign borrowing with long-term debt in which institutional constraints discipline clientelistic transfers and shape default incentives. Variation in institutional strength generates both emerging-market and developed-economy outcomes within a unified framework and accounts for heterogeneous post-democratization trajectories in emerging markets.

title: Corporate Governance as Bloodsport
affiliations: Drake University - Law School and University of Wyoming College of Law

detail.title: Corporate Governance as Bloodsport
detail.abstract:
The modern Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) movement promotes diversion of corporate assets from shareholders to “stakeholders.” This is done in the name of a corporate duty to society. But “successful” ESG efforts threaten the success of the corporate form by inviting rent-seeking. This conflict between ESG principles and established theories and norms of corporate law is difficult to resolve because corporate law lacks the tools needed to understand the type of collective decision-making that occurs in the corporate setting. This Article is the first to apply public choice economics—the economic study of collective decision-making—to corporate decision-making to identify the special interests that seek to divert resources through the rent-seeking process.

The resource to be diverted—the corporate residuum—is owned by the corporate shareholders. This fact is axiomatic in the bankruptcy context, where shareholders must wait at the end of the line to make their residual claim on remaining corporate assets. But shareholders own the residuum from the moment they form their corporate enterprise. Additionally, because shareholders are unable effectively to block attempts to steal their assets, the corporate residuum is subject to a commons problem. That problem raises the potential for the commons to be depleted, which would lead to investors fleeing public corporations, to the detriment of the financial system as a whole.

This Article is the first to draw on the work of Elinor Ostrom, the first female Nobel Prize winner in economics, to show that institutions—fiduciary duties, shareholder wealth maximization, and the business judgment rule—have arisen to forestall depletion of the commons, but that these institutions have been under attack for decades. Without care, they will fall, the corporate residual commons will be depleted, and the corporate form may fail.

title: Evolutionary AI in Practice: Japan's Bottom-Up Innovation Model and the Co-Evolution of Industrial and Competition Policy

detail.title: Evolutionary AI in Practice: Japan's Bottom-Up Innovation Model and the Co-Evolution of Industrial and Competition Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Funding: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: Funder Statement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This Article argues that Japan's trajectory in artificial intelligence is best understood as an evolutionary process in which bottom-up deployment of AI across industrial and service domains co-evolves with a policy framework that integrates restrained industrial support and anticipatory competition enforcement. In contrast to the centralized foundation-model strategies pursued in the United States and China and the regulatory-led framework emerging in the European Union, Japan's approach highlights how sustained deployment, domain specialization, and incremental learning can reshape both industrial structure and the focus of competition policy. Drawing on developments across robotics, manufacturing, mobility, and enterprise software, the Article introduces the concept of the deployment layer to explain how value creation and competitive bottlenecks increasingly arise at the interfaces through which AI systems are operationalized rather than within models alone. This perspective reframes industrial policy debates by suggesting that compute access, experimental deployment, and organizational learning may matter more than large-scale frontier-model subsidies, while competition policy must increasingly address control over data, infrastructure, and integration pathways. The Article concludes that Japan’s experience illustrates an alternative governance model for AI in which industrial policy and competition enforcement evolve together through iterative market learning, offering a framework for understanding AI governance as a process of policy co-evolution rather than discrete regulatory intervention.

title: The Evolution of National Social Dialogue in Europe under the Single Market, 1992-2006

detail.title: The Evolution of National Social Dialogue in Europe under the Single Market, 1992-2006
detail.abstract: This paper examines the evoluation of national social dialogue (bipartite wage bargaining) across European countries. Several commentators in the 1990s expected the dismantling of national social dialogue institutions. Following the liberalisation of markets, intensification of competition, and declining union power, bargaining structures were supposed to converge to the Anglo-Saxon model of decentralised bargaining. The paper seeks to gauge the plausibility of the ‘decentralization thesis’ using novel indicators of collective bargaining centralization across the EU15. It is shown that despite the changes in product markets, flexible working, and declining union density, a generalized decentralization of bargaining did not occur. Instead, in many European cases there is a counter-trend of centralization, which casts doubt to the decentralization thesis.

title: Labor Market Adjustments in the Medium Run: Female Labor Supply Five Years After the Pandemic
affiliations: The University of Tokyo

detail.title: Labor Market Adjustments in the Medium Run: Female Labor Supply Five Years After the Pandemic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declar no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The survey was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of the Tokyo Foundation (Approval No. 2025010001). I received informed consent electronically: Prior to participation, respondents were informed that the survey was anonymous and that their responses would be used exclusively for research purposes. Only those who agreed proceeded to the questionnaire.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded by the Tokyo Foundation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how female labor supply in Japan evolved in the medium run following the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a retrospective individual panel survey covering 2014, 2019, and 2024, I analyze employment, working hours, and income five years after the pandemic. On average, labor outcomes follow pre-pandemic trends, but substantial heterogeneity emerges across groups. Mothers of young children increased employment but reduced working hours, indicating adjustments along extensive and intensive margins. Remote workers also worked fewer hours, and the income gap between regular and non-regular workers widened. These findings suggest persistent changes in work arrangements and inequality in the post-pandemic labor market.

title: Network Services Liberalisation, Competition and Labour Market Governance: The Case of Greek Telecommunications

detail.title: Network Services Liberalisation, Competition and Labour Market Governance: The Case of Greek Telecommunications
detail.abstract: The paper traces the process of change in the regulation and associational governance of the labour market of the Greek telecommunications industry during the past two decades. The industry has been shaped by the EU regulatory impact, which prompted the opening up of the market to competition. The competitive pressures, in conjunction with the privatization process of the incumbent operator, brought about new structures of interest representation in labour and business. The paper considers these developments in the context of theoretical conjectures about convergence and divergence in the labour relations sphere of capitalist models. It is argued that the path of convergence to the Anglo-Saxon model of decentralised bargaining is largely explained by the form of interest representation of business, and the divisions between and within labour.

title: Plausible Pairwise Stability
affiliations: Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics

detail.title: Plausible Pairwise Stability
detail.abstract: I propose a stability concept for network formation under incomplete information. A network is plausibly pairwise stable if players' beliefs are consistent with common knowledge that the network is pairwise stable. I provide a condition for when plausibly pairwise stable networks exhibit clustering. In a model of vertical differentiation, I characterize the exact structure of minimally plausibly pairwise stable networks. They tend to be more segregated and contain more isolated players than pairwise stable networks. I discuss how incomplete information resolves the tension between stability and efficiency when there are negative linking externalities.

title: Overconfidence, Financial Literacy, and Crypto Asset Ownership in Europe - FIRSA Working Paper No. 2026/01

detail.title: Overconfidence, Financial Literacy, and Crypto Asset Ownership in Europe - FIRSA Working Paper No. 2026/01

declarations.funderStatement: This working paper series publishes early research results and policy papers connected to the EU Horizon Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions ERA Fellowship FIRSA. FIRSA is funded by the European Union under grant agreement No. 101180601 titled: Understanding FinTech Regulatory Sandbox Development in Europe. Views expressed are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect those of Vilnius University or the European Union.

detail.abstract: The role of financial literacy and overconfidence bias in shaping crypto-asset ownership remains empirically unresolved, with prior studies reporting conflicting results across countries and survey instruments. This paper advances the literature by providing harmonized EU-wide evidence on how subjective and objective financial literacy, overconfidence, digital confidence, and advisory trust predict crypto-asset ownership. Using individual-level data from the 2023 Flash Eurobarometer for 27 EU Member States, we estimate weighted logit models with country fixed effects and clustered standard errors. The results show that higher objective and subjective financial knowledge are consistently associated with a higher probability of owning crypto-assets, whereas overconfidence, measured as miscalibration between perceived and observed knowledge, is associated with a lower probability of ownership. Digital confidence exerts a large and robust positive effect while confidence in financial advisers has a mixed association with ownership. In contrast to the extant literature on the relationship between overconfidence and crypto-asset ownership, these findings suggest that retail crypto adoption in Europe is driven more by knowledge and perceived digital competence than by miscalibration.

title: Pro-natalist Fertility Policy and Female Analysts: Consequences and Remedies *
affiliations: Guangdong University of Finance and Economics, Guangdong University of Finance and Economics, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Pro-natalist Fertility Policy and Female Analysts: Consequences and Remedies *
detail.abstract: This paper examines the labor market consequences of nationwide pro-natalist policies and explores potential mitigating mechanisms. Leveraging China's relaxation of its decades-long One-Child Policy as a quasi-natural experiment, we show a 7.45% decrease in forecast accuracy among female analysts of reproductive age compared to their male counterparts. This motherhood penalty is more pronounced in provinces with stronger fertility norms and for firms that are more difficult to forecast. Moreover, we explore a broad set of potential remedies. Our results suggest that fostering a gender equality culture and expanding access to childcare resources that enhance family-career compatibility can mitigate this negative effect. In contrast, policies that focus primarily on extending maternity leave appear to exacerbate the productivity gap, likely due to the career interruptions that may erode their professional skills and connections. Ultimately, these productivity declines contribute to longer career gaps and higher attrition rates among female analysts, highlighting critical trade-offs between fertility-promoting policies and women's professional advancement.

title: Detecting Lies When Truth is Unobservable
affiliations: UCLA Anderson and ESCP Business School

detail.title: Detecting Lies When Truth is Unobservable
detail.abstract: When agents hide bad outcomes, they leave a statistical fingerprint: downside variation shrinks faster than total variation. We formalise this through two compression statistics-Cσ, which measures volatility compression (the standard deviation of reported outcomes), and Cρ, the ratio of downside semivariance to total variance—each falling by an amount determined exactly by manipulation intensity. Fat-tailed data demand much larger samples for equivalent power; kurtosis inflates the null variance linearly. A four-level identification hierarchy separates genuine manipulation from legitimate smoothing—and no smoothing strategy simultaneously fools both Cσ and Cρ. A direct corollary: return smoothing inflates the Sortino ratio strictly more than the Sharpe ratio. The test requires no external benchmark—practical for screening hedge funds, corporate earnings, and national accounts.

title: Ease of Doing Business in the U.S. – A Tax Perspective
affiliations: Boston University, School of Law

detail.title: Ease of Doing Business in the U.S. – A Tax Perspective
detail.abstract:
From incorporation to capitalization and eventual redemption, the tax rules surrounding a corporation trace the practical life of a startup. A founder rarely begins with liquidity; value exists instead in ideas, property, or early effort. The legal question is therefore not how much tax is owed, but when it becomes appropriate to impose it. U.S. corporate tax provisions generally postpone recognition at the moment of organization and instead attach consequences to later realization. This ordering allows a venture to take form, admit collaborators, and attempt commercialization before taxation converts paper value into a cash obligation. The structure does not eliminate tax. It determines the stage at which economic activity becomes mature enough to bear it.


This article follows that progression. It begins with formation, explaining how contributions become ownership rather than gain, and then turns to hiring, where equity compensation substitutes for salary and aligns incentives during the resource-constrained phase. The discussion next addresses distributions, examining how earnings and profits measure a corporation’s real capacity to pay and govern the character of payouts. Finally, it considers exits, analyzing when redemptions and buybacks constitute a sale rather than a dividend. Taken together, these rules form a consistent sequence in which taxation generally follows realized value, providing founders operational flexibility while preserving the integrity of the tax base once economic outcomes are no longer uncertain.

title: Communism as Systemic Health: A Post-Capitalist Grammar
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Communism as Systemic Health: A Post-Capitalist Grammar

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The left excels at critiquing capital's pathologies but lacks a language for social h ealth. This article supplies one. Reformulating communism not as a utopia but as a dy namic attractor of systemic health, it posits a "projectionentropy" framework to diagnose capitalism as an entropyrunaway engine. Evidence from financialised housing, carbon markets and enclosed A I points to a precipice: the system's health probability has plummeted from 0.62 to 0.3 1 in four years. The alternative is a postscarcity society characterised by low entropy and high coherence. This vision demand s a new political strategy: parametric assaults on the dominant institutional matrix. Th e article maps three such assaultsfrom financial disarmament to cognitive emancipationand stakes its claim on a falsifiable prediction. The goal is to equip the left not with an other critique, but with a quantitative science for building a viable future.

title: Weaponization of the Land and Property Rights System in the Syrian Civil War: Facilitating Restitution?

detail.title: Weaponization of the Land and Property Rights System in the Syrian Civil War: Facilitating Restitution?
detail.abstract: The Syrian civil war has seen the weaponization of its land and property rights system by the primary combatant groups in the country. The government is the most robust in its use of the tenure system to locate, target, destroy, confiscate, cleanse, and gain revenue by way of the institutions and attributes comprising the system. Based on fieldwork with Syrian refugees in Lebanon, Jordan, and Turkey, this article describes seven ways the Syrian government is currently using the land and property rights system in its military-on-civilian engagements. While the objective of such use is presumably to permanently prevail over opposition civilian constituencies, the article describes how this actually creates evidence usable for effective restitution of lands and properties subsequent to the war.

title: The AfCFTA Agreement: Origins, Legal Structure, Key Features, and Institutions
affiliations: School of Law, University of the Witwatersrand

detail.title: The AfCFTA Agreement: Origins, Legal Structure, Key Features, and Institutions
detail.abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a legal, institutional and operational system. I begin by outlining the Agreement’s negotiation history and treaty structure, including the phased development of Protocols on trade in goods, trade in services, investment, intellectual property, competition policy, digital trade, and women and youth in trade. Moreover, I analyze the substantive features of the AfCFTA Agreement and its Protocols, highlighting their regulatory scope, internal architecture and relationship to African integration objectives. I then examine the governance institutions established under the Agreement – the Assembly, Council of Ministers, Committee of Senior Trade Officials and the Secretariat – together with the dispute settlement mechanism. In a further section, I review the operational instruments, implementation tools and Secretariat-led initiatives that support the transition from treaty commitments to actual trade, including the African Trade Observatory, digital NTB mechanism, PAPSS, adjustment facilities and the Guided Trade Initiative. The chapter concludes by situating the AfCFTA within Africa’s broader integration trajectory and the wider evolution of global trade governance.

title: Constitutive vs. Corrective: A Causal Taxonomy of Human Runtime Involvement in AI Systems
affiliations: and University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute

detail.title: Constitutive vs. Corrective: A Causal Taxonomy of Human Runtime Involvement in AI Systems

declarations.funderStatement: Kevin Baum was supported by the German Research Founda- tion (DFG) under grant No. 389792660, as part of TRR 248, see https://perspicuous- computing.science,bytheGermanFederalMinistryofEducationandResearch(BMBF) as part of the project MAC-MERLin (Grant Agreement No. 16IW24007), and by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and the Saarland within the scope of (To)CERTAIN (Project ID EFRE-AuF-0000942). Johann Laux was supported by a British Academy Postdoctoral Fellowship (grant no. PF22\220076) and the article is a deliverable of the "The Emerging Laws of Oversight" project.

detail.abstract: As AI systems increasingly permeate high-stakes decisionmaking, the terminology regarding human involvement-Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL), and Human Oversighthas become vexingly ambiguous. This ambiguity complicates interdisciplinary collaboration between computer science, law, philosophy, psychology, and sociology and can lead to regulatory uncertainty. We propose a clarification grounded in causal structure, focused on human involvement during the runtime of AI systems. The distinction between HITL and HOTL, we argue, is not primarily spatial but causal: HITL is constitutive (a human contribution is necessary for the decision output), while HOTL is corrective (external to the primary causal chain, capable of preventing or modifying outputs). Within HOTL, we distinguish three temporal modes-synchronous, asynchronous, and anticipatorysituated within a nested model of provider and deployer runtime that clarifies their different capacities for intervention. A second, orthogonal dimension captures cognitive integration: whether human and machine operate as complementary or hybrid intelligence, yielding four structurally distinct configurations. Finally, we distinguish these descriptive categories from the normative requirements they serve: statutory "Human Oversight" is a specific normative mode of HOTL that demands not merely a corrective causal position, but genuine preparedness and capacity for effective intervention. Because the same person may occupy both HITL and HOTL roles simultaneously, we argue that this role duality must be treated as a design problem requiring architectural and epistemic mitigation rather than mere acknowledgment.

title: The Often Unseen Price of Suboptimal Optimum

detail.title: The Often Unseen Price of Suboptimal Optimum

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the System Adjusted Payoff Model (SAPM), a continuous measurement framework for quantifying system-destructive cooperation in strategic environments. SAPM provides three computable instruments: system beta B_W = -dW/dΠ (systemic welfare loss per unit of private gain), shadow price u* = 1/B_W, and crossover time T* = S/nh (when degradation becomes irreversible).

title: Rural Land Tenure Resilience in Postwar Syria: Implications for Restitution and Stabilization

detail.title: Rural Land Tenure Resilience in Postwar Syria: Implications for Restitution and Stabilization
detail.abstract: The impending close to the war in Syria brings to the fore the prospect of approximately 13 million forcibly displaced people considering returns to places of origin in the country. However the reattachment of people to their housing, land and property (HLP) faces a daunting set of challenges-the prospect of demographic change, the application of expropriation laws, confiscations and political agendas. Greatly aggravating these challenges is the reality that there will now not be an internationally supervised and financed HLP restitution process applying accepted international conventions of transitional justice, rule of law and human rights as is the norm after wars. Instead, forms of land tenure resilience will become a primary influence in facilitating restitution and strengthening tenure security. With a focus on rural Syria, this article examines three forms of tenurial resilience which are likely to play a large role in the stabilization and recovery of the country, and explores opportunities for supporting these.

title: Use of Upgraded Evidence in Cadaster Approaches for Syrian Refugee Return

detail.title: Use of Upgraded Evidence in Cadaster Approaches for Syrian Refugee Return
detail.abstract: The enormity of the Syrian refugee crisis in Turkey, Jordan and Lebanon, together with the difficulties of their livelihoods and the burden placed on host countries, highlights the importance of planning now for the eventual return of refugees to their housing, land and property (HLP) in Syria. As in all refugee generating scenarios, the manner in which most Syrians departed their HLP resulted in little opportunity to obtain, prepare or bring, the documentation needed prove ownership, occupation, or claim to their properties to which they must one day return. Further, in a great many cases such documentation, if it existed, was incomplete, inaccurate, contested, confused, improperly recorded and of uncertain legal standing. Overlain on this situation is a long history of land and property confiscations, dispossession, grievance, corruption and patronage, which has meant that many HLP assets will be reclaimed anew when their former occupants return. While the social and legal challenges for reattaching returning refugees to their HLP is difficult in any postwar situation, this will be particularly so in the Syrian case due to the absence of documentation and the contested, confused and aggrieved land rights system in the country's history.

title: Role-Based Legal Cognition Modeling Infrastructure - Why Generative AI Cannot Replace Legal Reasoning

detail.title: Role-Based Legal Cognition Modeling Infrastructure - Why Generative AI Cannot Replace Legal Reasoning

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in legal systems has traditionally focused on workflow automation and efficiency gains for law firms, emphasizing document processing, predictive analytics, and operational optimization. While such applications improve productivity, they rarely engage the structural foundations of legal reasoning necessary for auditable, court-defensible outcomes. This paper introduces Role-Based Legal Cognition Modeling (RLCM), a framework for structuring AI legal reasoning around institutional roles, responsibilities, procedural rules, and jurisdictionally validated corpora. By embedding deterministic, auditable cognition pathways, RLCM produces legally grounded, traceable outputs aligned with codified statutes and procedural norms, while respecting cultural and institutional context. The framework situates RLCM in historical and global contexts, referencing European initiatives such as AI4Intelligence and early Latin American applications. Unlike AI4Intelligence, which emphasizes forensic admissibility, RLCM focuses on deterministic, role-based legal reasoning within civil law institutions, supporting auditability for courts, clerks, students, and civic stakeholders. Operational deployment in Guatemala provided illustrative validation, demonstrating that RLCM can structure deterministic, auditable reasoning in civil law scenarios while encoding procedural discretion and local norms, offering preliminary methodological insights for real-world applicability.

title: Do Banks Fully Price Biodiversity Risk?
affiliations: University of Venice - Department of Economics, ICMA Centre, Henley Business School, University of Reading, ICMA Centre - Henley Business School, University of Reading, University of Reading - ICMA Centre, Natural History Museum and Natural History Museum

detail.title: Do Banks Fully Price Biodiversity Risk?
detail.abstract: We investigate whether banks fully incorporate biodiversity risk into loan pricing using a large sample of securitised loans to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Europe. Combining loan-level data from European DataWarehouse with high-resolution biodiversity indicators from the Natural History Museum, we construct a borrower-level measure of biodiversity risk across time and space. Our empirical strategy jointly examines the relationship between biodiversity risk, credit risk, and loan pricing. First, we document that biodiversity loss is significantly associated with higher loan spreads, suggesting that banks do account for this risk in lending rates. Second, and most importantly, we find that biodiversity loss is positively associated with default probabilities even after controlling for loan spreads, indicating that biodiversity risk contains information not fully captured by banks' pricing decisions. These findings provide novel evidence of partial pricing: while biodiversity risk is reflected in loan spreads, it is not fully internalised, offering new insights into the efficiency of risk pricing in SME lending markets. Economically, a one-standard-deviation increase in biodiversity loss raises the probability of default by about 12 basis points, corresponding to a 14.8% increase relative to the sample average, implying a meaningful increase in firms' default risk.

title: Communicating with Data-Generating Processes: An Experimental Analysis
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Economics and Princeton University

detail.title: Communicating with Data-Generating Processes: An Experimental Analysis
detail.abstract: In many applications, agents can more easily influence how data are generated than manipulate the data themselves. For example, students choose which classes to take but cannot modify their grades once assigned, and firms determine how performance indicators are calculated rather than directly altering results. This paper experimentally studies information transmission when data are generated through an unobservable, strategically chosen process. We focus on settings where an informed sender—such as a student or a firm—privately selects a data-generating process (DGP)—a portfolio of classes or an accounting methodology—to shape the beliefs of an uninformed receiver, such as an employer or an investor. Across treatments, we vary which DGPs are feasible and whether some come at a cost. These variations span different levels of information verifiability and allow us to capture, within a unified framework, the core insights of disclosure, cheap-talk, and signaling models. Our findings reveal three main patterns. First, while senders select their DGPs strategically in line with theoretical predictions, receivers often fail to account for this strategic selection. Second, introducing differential costs across feasible DGPs mitigates this DGP selection neglect. Third, while receivers’ biases are robust across environments, their consequences vary: information transmission falters most when the evidence receivers observe is highly sensitive to the sender’s DGP choices. Finally, increasing transparency about the selected DGP—a policy often advocated in practice—does not, in general, improve information transmission.

title: A Joint Online Learning Framework for Time-Varying Parameter Correction and Multi-Scale Signal Decay - Unified Theory for Adaptive Factor Portfolio Optimization

detail.title: A Joint Online Learning Framework for Time-Varying Parameter Correction and Multi-Scale Signal Decay - Unified Theory for Adaptive Factor Portfolio Optimization
detail.abstract: Factor signals decay at heterogeneous rates, and this heterogeneity is itself state-dependent: during market crises, the information half-life of momentum signals collapses from roughly six weeks to under four days, while value signals retain nearly 90% of their predictive power. Ignoring this asymmetry causes systematic portfolio mispricing that is most severe precisely when correct allocation matters most. We develop a Joint Online Learning Framework (JOLF) that tracks state-dependent decay rates in real time via a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter, jointly estimated with regime identification and higher-moment corrections in a single recursive Bayesian sweep.

title: The Minimum Wage Poverty Trap: A Theoretical Analysis

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding how minimum wage policies may create a "poverty trap" that reduces low-wage workers' incentives to invest in human capital. While minimum wage increases provide immediate income benefits, beyond a certain threshold they diminish expected returns to education and training, thereby reducing occupational mobility. I formalize this relationship through a utility maximization model incorporating time discounting, opportunity costs, and uncertainty. The framework derives explicit conditions under which an inverted-U relationship emerges between minimum wage levels and human capital investment, including bounded skill premia, education affordability constraints, and wagedependent present bias. Recent empirical work by Alessandrini and Milla (2024) provides partial support, finding minimum wage increases lead to higher community college enrollment but lower university enrollment, consistent with the model's predictions. The analysis contributes to minimum wage policy debates by highlighting potential trade-offs between short-term income support and long-term economic mobility, suggesting complementary policies are needed.

title: Relative-Value Reversal in Precious Metals and Mining ETFs

detail.title: Relative-Value Reversal in Precious Metals and Mining ETFs
detail.abstract: This paper studies reversal and relative-value strategies in precious metals and mining equities, with a focus on gold, silver, and junior versus senior mining ETFs. I first test a baseline cross-sectional reversal strategy across a universe of precious-metals-related mining equities. I then test benchmark-adjusted residual reversal and several ETF spread reversal strategies, including junior-versus-senior miner spreads and miner-versus-metal spreads. Strategy performance is evaluated across multiple lookback horizons using annualized return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, turnover, and implied holding period, with transaction costs explicitly incorporated. The results show that raw cross-sectional miner reversal and residual miner reversal are weak after costs, while ETF-based relative-value reversal performs materially better. The strongest strategy is the reversal of junior silver miners relative to silver itself, represented by the SILJ-SLV spread, with the best net Sharpe ratio of 0.541 at a 10-day horizon. Overall, the evidence suggests that relative-value reversal is more robust than raw standalone reversal, and that silver-based dislocations are stronger than comparable gold-based dislocations.

title: Bitcoin Exit Dominance in Monetary Coordination Games

detail.title: Bitcoin Exit Dominance in Monetary Coordination Games
detail.abstract: In a multipolar world with no trusted monetary coordinator, how do rational actors settle large-value transactions across trust boundaries? We model this as a non-cooperative game—the "Exit Game"—in which capital allocators choose between capturable settlement systems ("Stay") and neutral settlement ("Exit"). The model rests on four empirical axioms: persistent multipolarity, rational self-interest, computational hardness, and network effect persistence. We prove three results. First, the payoff advantage of Exit over Stay is strictly increasing in adoption: every term in the payoff differential favors Exit under maintained monotonicity conditions, and each actor's adoption threshold approaches zero under structural debasement (Theorem 1). Second, no coalition can sustain coordinated Stay, because permissionless access makes defection costless and the first defector captures fleeing capital (Theorem 2). Third, the resulting equilibrium is absorbing: the monotone adoption process converges to full adoption once a critical mass is reached, because trust conditions required for coordinated return cannot be reestablished (Theorem 3). The model is explicitly falsifiable: six conditions are identified under which the central claims would fail. Bitcoin is the unique asset satisfying the necessary properties for neutral settlement—a result proved by systematic elimination across seven asset classes in Hash (2026b).

title: Research on Infrared Thermal Fault Detection for Transformer Bushings Based on the LTF-YOLO Algorithm
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

detail.title: Research on Infrared Thermal Fault Detection for Transformer Bushings Based on the LTF-YOLO Algorithm
detail.abstract: Transformer bushings are critical insulation components in power systems, and early diagnosis of thermal faults is essential for safe and reliable operation. Traditional infrared inspection methods depend heavily on expert experience and are inefficient, while existing deep learning approaches often struggle with small hot spots, weak temperature contrast, and complex backgrounds, resulting in missed detections and false alarms. To address these issues, this study proposes a lightweight infrared fault detection algorithm, LTF-YOLO.Built on the YOLOv8n baseline, the proposed method introduces three improvements. A parameter-free SimAM attention module is embedded in the backbone to enhance the representation of weak thermal features. A DySample dynamic upsampling mechanism is adopted to improve feature reconstruction and contour recovery for small-scale targets. In addition, a C2f-MSDA module is designed to capture multi-scale contextual information, enabling joint modeling of local details and global temperature rise patterns.Experiments on a self-constructed infrared image dataset of transformer bushings show that LTF-YOLO achieves a mean average precision of 0.951, improving detection accuracy by 6.25% over the baseline YOLOv8 model with only a slight increase in parameters. In complex scenes, the improvement further reaches 9.07%. Ablation and comparative experiments further verify the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

title: Local Health Shocks and the Cost of Equity Capital: Evidence from the Opioid Epidemic

detail.title: Local Health Shocks and the Cost of Equity Capital: Evidence from the Opioid Epidemic
detail.abstract: This study examines whether localized public health shocks affect firms’ implied cost of equity capital (ICC) by exploiting variation in county-level opioid mortality. Using 19,421 firm-year observations from 2003 to 2023, we show that firms headquartered in areas with higher opioid mortality face significantly higher ICC, with effects that are more pronounced in manufacturing industries. Cross-sectional analyses indicate that the effect is stronger for labor-intensive firms and weaker for firms with higher R&D intensity, consistent with a labor supply disruption channel through which local health shocks increase the risk priced in the cost of capital. An instrumental variable approach based on opioid dispensing rates and a difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered adoption of state-level Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) consistently yield consistent results.

detail.abstract: Solar adoption is now large enough that small efficiency losses translate into material economic and emissions impacts. A major, addressable source of loss is photovoltaic (PV) soiling. Dust, pollen, and biofilms reduce output and, in some cases, persist through rainfall. This paper proposes a low-cost "solar flagging" intervention: inverter and monitoring platforms would identify systems with statistically meaningful underperformance (e.g., sustained ≥6% annual production gap versus an expected baseline), and notify owners when cleaning is likely to be economically justified. The approach is targeted: most systems would not be flagged, but heavy-soiling and rain-persistent sites could recover meaningful energy, reduce customer bills, and avoid emissions. The proposal leverages data already collected at scale to create measurement-based cleaning schedules.

title: Authenticity in Corporate Social Performance: Employee-ESG Disagreement and its Financial Consequences
affiliations: University of Innsbruck and University of Innsbruck

detail.title: Authenticity in Corporate Social Performance: Employee-ESG Disagreement and its Financial Consequences
detail.abstract: We contrast external ESG Social Pillar scores with the internal assessments of workplace experiences of employees to analyze the authenticity of corporate social performance. We find limited and inconsistent alignment between ESG Social Pillar scores and employee-reported workplace satisfaction on the aggregate level as well as within subcategories of social performance, which are most relevant to employees. We further find that the employee-ESG disagreement is reflected in stock market valuations, as firms with higher disagreement display larger risk premia. Finally, we link disagreement to firms' governance characteristics and show that weaker governance structures tend to increase disagreements. Overall, the findings support the role of employee-based information as a distinct internal benchmark for assessing the authenticity of corporate social performance.

detail.abstract: Applying XAI methods to time series forecasting is hindered by the nonstationary nature of temporal data. Existing research relies on fixed sliding windows or assumptions of monotonic feature decay, often yielding explanations that are mathematically coherent but semantically misaligned with the underlying data generating process. We introduce Adaptive WIN-SHAP, a framework that employs the Local Parametric Approach (LPA) to dynamically identify Intervals of Homogeneity (temporal spans where model parameters remain statistically stable) using Likelihood Ratio Tests to replace heuristic window selection with a statistically grounded, adaptive mechanism. We evaluate the method through a simulation study on a process with known regime changes, a robustness analysis along six dimensions, and an empirical application to the electricity market. Quantitative benchmarks demonstrate that Adaptive WIN-SHAP achieves competitive or superior performance relative to existing baselines across perturbation-based faithfulness and MIF/LIF ablation ratios. The empirical application validates these findings in a real-world non-stationary setting, where the adaptive window produces interpretable regime dynamics and near-optimal faithfulness with strong feature discrimination. These results suggest that aligning the explanation window with the homogeneous regime of the data can meaningfully improve interpretability, moving time-series XAI toward a more principled, adaptive framework.

detail.abstract: Our study investigated the size of the gender pay gap in the American advertising industry, controlling for all known factors that explain a gap. We found women were paid 5% less than men, and 8% less if they were mothers. While most men and women believe in the existence of a gender pay gap, they both overestimate its size, with men closer in estimating the industry's true size, and women closer in estimating the size of the general population pay gap. Further, women believed they were personally immune from a pay gap, when in fact, the average woman is losing $271,829 over her career due to gender. The role of social dynamics was also investigated, which found male managers were more likely to stop pay equity progress for women through unresponsiveness, as well as the finding that men who are uncomfortable working with women were paid more.

title: Non-parametric Identification of Dynamic Treatment Effects: a Graphical Approach to Causality

detail.title: Non-parametric Identification of Dynamic Treatment Effects: a Graphical Approach to Causality
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified framework to study different types of dynamic treatment effects (DTE), extending the dynamic potential outcome (DPO) framework developed by Torgovitsky (2019). The DPO framework is used to study the causal effect of the immediate preceding past on the present in his paper. In this paper, I first show that DTE such as the causal effect of the distant past on the present can be non-parametrically identified in a DPO framework which does not necessarily assume that the distant past enters the function of the present potential response. I then develop an algorithm leveraging a novel graphical representation of the DPO model. This graph-based algorithm provides a computationally tractable means of scaling the DPO framework beyond binary variables to multi-valued variables, circumventing the curse of dimensionality inherent in dynamic treatment effect studies.

title: Systemic Governance Risk in AI Agent Networks: Cross-Institutional Contagion and Topological Vulnerability

detail.title: Systemic Governance Risk in AI Agent Networks: Cross-Institutional Contagion and Topological Vulnerability

The methodology described in this paper informs the company's commercial offerings. The dataset, findings, and analytical framework are presented independently of commercial considerations.

detail.abstract:
Prior work established that AI agent governance within individual financial institutions exhibits a topological structure in which governance failure propagates through cascade dynamics (Collins, 2026a; Collins, 2026b). This paper extends the analysis from the institution to the system. Using 239 financial institutions, 44,888 AI agents, and 147,559 typed edges across 43 countries, we construct a cross-institutional dependency layer comprising 52,652 pairwise institutional links through 74 shared external technology vendors.

The findings follow a three-stage pattern. First, the shared surface: a single technology vendor is present across 99.2% of sampled institutions, and more than a third of all cross-institutional links connect two institutions that both score below 5.0 on governance. Second, the concentrated architecture: the mean Gini coefficient of governance node degree distribution is 0.419, and 7.1% of institutions exhibit single-point-of-failure governance where more than half of all oversight edges route through one node. Third, the bottleneck paradox: governance concentration exceeds vendor concentration in 82% of institutions. The committee that assesses vendor risk is itself a greater single point of failure than the vendor it assesses.

Three formal hypotheses are tested. Robustness analysis confirms that the SPOF finding is stable across threshold sensitivity (40%: 31 institutions; 50%: 17; 60%: 9) and that governance concentration is structural across all sectors (Gini range 0.389–0.425).

title: Institutional Failure Modes: A Configurational Theory of Institutional Reproduction and Fragility
